en: In the first fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*, there are ten kinds of differences in characteristics.
[The following] are their names. Although the names are [as follows], of the first two types...
The names of the [first] five are established based on their modes of activity (*ākāra*);
the latter five are established based on the substance of their activity.
"Activity" (*caryā*) refers to the practice performed by the practitioner; it is that which serves as the basis for reliance.
Regarding the second point, the characteristics to be known:
the first meaning is similar to the preceding [explanation].
Furthermore, there is another interpretation.
That which is associated with the three knowledges is called "that which should be known.
Regarding the characteristics [of the entry], understanding that which accords with [the truth] is termed "entry.
The fourth entry concerns cause and effect.
The first section is titled "Names and Designations for Realization.
Regarding the fifth [section], "Cause and Effect":
the various distinct names are termed "differentiation" (*viśeṣa*).
Regarding the sixth point, the characteristics of relying on the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*):
"relying" (*niśraya*) refers to the arising [of practice] based upon the Dharma;
furthermore, it refers to the arising of cultivation based upon the true precepts.
To prevent what is improper and cease from evil is called "precept" (śīla).
To advance and seek within principle is termed "study" (śikṣā).
To distinguish the great from the small is named the "distinguished superior characteristic."
Seventh, regarding the characteristics of training based on the mind:
"based" (niśraya) refers to relying upon dharmas;
furthermore, it is called "based" because one relies upon true meditative concentration (samādhi) to initiate cultivation.
Not dispersing while relying on principle is called "training based on the mind.
Distinguishing the Great Vehicle from the Small Vehicle is called the "distinguished superior characteristic.
The eighth is "training based on wisdom."
The mind’s reliance upon the Dharma is called "reliance";
furthermore, relying upon true wisdom to give rise to contemplation is called "reliance.
Thoroughly illuminating and penetrating the two truths is called "wisdom."
The superior characteristic of differentiation is defined as the great being distinct from the small.
Regarding the ninth, the superior characteristic of the quiescence that is the fruit of training:
it is called "fruit" because it is the recompense for causes.
The fruit realized through causes is termed the "fruit of training" (śaikṣaphala);
the immovability of the dharma-nature is termed "quiescence" (śānta);
and the fruit-virtue that is free from marks is designated as "cessation" (nirodha).
Surpassing the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) is called the "distinguished characteristic of superiority.
Regarding the tenth, the "characteristic of the distinction of wisdom" (*jñāna-viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*):
definitive discernment is termed "wisdom."
Distinguishing between cause and fruit is called "differentiation" (*viśeṣa*).
Distinguishing the great from the small is also called "differentiation. Question:
Are these ten characteristics taught in a single sūtra?
Regarding the fact that this is taught collectively in many sutras,
there are two interpretations.
First, according to the beginning of the treatise, it appears to be taught in a single sutra.
Therefore, the *Asamasamavyākaraṇa-parivarta* states:
"In the presence of the Buddha, the World-Honored One,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva skillfully enters into the meaning of the phrases and even speaks these words."
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten superior characteristics that surpass other teachings and the like.
Below, these ten names are listed in detail, and their characteristics are extensively explained.
Therefore, while it appears that [the ten meanings] are taught in a single sutra,
when verified against the extensive text below, they appear to be found in many sutras;
thus, under the "Chapter on Various Names," the author extensively cites many sutras and treatises to establish these ten meanings.
For what reason is it so? These two texts should be examined;
they briefly expound ten topics within the Abhidharma Piṭaka.
These are precisely those discussed in the "Chapter on Peerless Sacred Teachings" and the "Chapter on the Sequence of the Ten Topics."
The ten meanings are explained in detail in other sūtras and treatises;
these are precisely those discussed from the section on "Various Names" down to the end of the treatise.
This is because the abbreviated text is contained within what is taught in a single sūtra.
The first two chapters provide a concise analysis and explanation based on a brief sutra,
as the extensive texts are scattered across many sutras and treatises.
Following the chapter on various names, the meaning will be explained in detail according to specific sutras and treatises.
Because these destinies exist, there are differences between the extensive and the abbreviated versions.
This meaning is profound and far-reaching; it is only fitting that its principles be investigated.
The explanation of the names and meanings is now complete.
Second, regarding the discernment of its essential nature (*svabhāva*),
there are two approaches.
The first is the approach of subsuming the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) into the reality (*tattva*).
The second is the gate of discussing the two characteristics in their reality.
Subsuming the characteristics into their reality,
all ten kinds of superior characteristics take the suchness of the three non-natures as their essence.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa-siṃha-parivarta* states:
"That which is neither cause nor effect is the fundamental nature of all dharmas;
its essence is eternally constant and unchanging."
The "Inquiry into the Sick" chapter of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states that non-abiding is the foundation;
its meaning is similar [to this].
The *Zhichachang* (Discrimination of Wisdom) states that suchness is the universal characteristic common to all dharmas.
Regarding the two characteristics discussed together as realities:
the first superior characteristic has the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) as its essence,
while the second superior characteristic has the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) as its essence.
The third superior characteristic has the wisdom of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) as its essence.
The fourth superior characteristic has the six perfections, both mundane and supramundane, as its essence.
The fifth superior characteristic has the ten stages (*bhūmi*) as its essence.
The sixth superior characteristic has the three aggregates as its essence;
the seventh characteristic has the four samādhis as its essence;
and the eighth characteristic has the four wisdoms as its essence.
These three trainings take both the preparatory cultivation and the actual cultivation based on conditions as their essence.
The ninth characteristic takes nirvana as its essence.
The tenth characteristic takes the three bodies (trikāya) as its essence.
This meaning is explained in detail as it is taught in the *Anupama-sūtra* and other authoritative scriptures.
Each of the ten meanings and their characteristics is analyzed extensively in its own separate chapter.
This concludes the second section on essential nature (*svabhāva*).
Third, regarding the clarification of the sequence,
there are two meanings.
First, the sequence is clarified by means of the ten dharmas.
Second, the sequence is elucidated in terms of the arising of practice.
Regarding the first point—the elucidation of the sequence based on the ten dharmas—there are two meanings.
The first is the differentiation of the sequence by means of three gates.
Second, the sequence is established by means of the ten dharmas.
Regarding the explanation of the sequence according to the three gates,
the *Cidi-zhang* (Chapter on Sequence) states:
The objects have a sequence;
the correct practice has a sequence;
and the fruit has a sequence.
Because the first two clarify the principles upon which the arising of practice depends, they are explained first; thus, the objects (*viṣaya*) have a sequential order.
Because practice arises based on these principles and accords with them rather than being erroneous, it is called "right practice" (*samyak-pratipatti*), which likewise has a sequential order.
Regarding the latter two, because cause and effect are established, they receive the name "fruit," and thus there is a sequence of fruits.
Furthermore, regarding the sequence of objects, there are two meanings:
first, the sequence is clarified in relation to subsequent practice.
Because it is able to give rise to practice, the principle is explained first.
Second, the sequence is clarified by means of the first two [stages]:
first, the superior characteristics of the basis clarify the equality of cause and effect.
Because they are the leaders of those who pervert [the truth], they are explained first in order to refute [views such as] the inequality of cause and effect.
Second, one should know that the principle of the existence and non-existence of the two truths is clarified in order to refute [the views of] fixed existence and non-existence.
Because this principle is subtler than the preceding ones, it is explained later.
Furthermore, regarding the sequence of the six right practices, there are three meanings:
first, distinguishing their order relative to what precedes them.
One initiates this practice based on the aforementioned principles and methods.
Second, the sequence is established in relation to what follows;
it is by means of this correct practice that one can give rise to the subsequent result.
Third, the sequence is distinguished based on the six practices.
Since the consciousness that takes objects as its conditions and relinquishes them is the primary gateway for entering reality, the characteristics of entry are explained first.
Because one observes that [phenomena] arise from causes and are further able to produce subsequent effects, the characteristics of cause and effect are clarified next.
Having clarified the differences in the characteristics of cultivation according to the ten stages, the next section clarifies the distinctions in the modes of cultivation.
Following that, the characteristics of the three trainings are clarified in order to distinguish the differences in the essential nature of the practices to be cultivated.
Among the three trainings, since ethical discipline (*śīla*) is able to prevent what is non-virtuous, the training in ethics is explained first.
Since meditative concentration (*samādhi*) quiets mental distraction, the training in mind is explained next.
Since wisdom (*prajñā*) severs ignorance, the training in wisdom is distinguished last.
The latter two fruits also possess two meanings:
first, they clarify the sequence in relation to the preceding [stages],
because these two fruits arise from the preceding correct practice.
Next, the sequence is established with respect to the two fruits.
Because the essence of the fruit of quiescence is primary, it is explained first;
because the function of the fruit of the differentiation of wisdom is secondary, it is explained later.

Regarding the three [natures] in this way, how are they applied to the ten? Since the principle of causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) can refute intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the first characteristic is first analyzed.
Based on the aforementioned causal conditions, the principle of the three natures that can refute existence and non-existence is clarified; next, it should be understood as follows.
Regarding the preceding section, one should know that after distinguishing the contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), the characteristics of entry (*praveśalakṣaṇa*) are clarified;
regarding the preceding characteristics of entry, after distinguishing the beginning and end of contemplation, cause and effect (*hetu-phala*) are clarified;
regarding the preceding fruit, after distinguishing the differences in its modes of activity (*ākāra*), the distinctions in cultivation (*bhāvanā-viśeṣa*) are clarified.
Since the preceding section has distinguished the essential nature of the practices to be cultivated, the next section clarifies the three trainings, beginning with morality (*śīla*).
Because the training in morality comes first, it is explained initially.
Since concentration (*samādhi*) arises from morality, the training in the mind (*citta-śikṣā*) is explained next.
Because wisdom arises from meditative concentration, the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*) is explained next.
Since delusions are severed by wisdom, the fruit of cessation (*nirodha-phala*) is explained next.
Because function arises based on the essence, the distinctions of wisdom (*jñāna-viśeṣa*) are explained next.
The sequential order has been explained with respect to the ten dharmas.
Second, regarding the sequential order of the arising of practice:
the first two give rise to understanding.
The next six give rise to practice,
while the final two give rise to aspiration;
thus there is a sequential order.
What is the meaning of this?
The first two [sections] distinguish the principles and teachings so that people may give rise to understanding.

Within the section on the characteristics of the basis, it clarifies the equality of cause and effect, thereby giving rise to right view and causing one to abandon the six types of partial attachment.

Second, one should understand that the characteristic of the teaching clarifying the principle that things are neither existent nor non-existent gives rise to the realization of the Middle Way, thereby abandoning the three types of slanderous mentalities:
namely, the three kinds of slander consisting of superimposition, denial, and contradiction.
Next, these six [verses] clarify the methods of practice, teaching people how to initiate their cultivation based upon them.
What is the meaning of this?
It extensively distinguishes the ritual procedures for cultivation, instructing people on what to practice, such as the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) and so forth.
This applies equally to the categories up to the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*).
Therefore, after the teaching on the six characteristics, one gives rise to practice;
next, by means of the two [characteristics], one gives rise to aspiration.
The teaching on the method for discerning the fruit gives rise to the aspiration [for nirvana];
the teaching on the supreme characteristic of quiescence seeks nirvana;
and the teaching on the superior characteristic of the differentiation of wisdom seeks bodhi.
What is the meaning of this?
It is to extensively discern the fruits and virtues of all Buddhas so that those sentient beings, having compared themselves with others, may seek their future fruition.
As stated in the "Section on Explaining the Name" (*Shiming-fen*) of the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages):
One gives rise to a joyful mind because one thinks, "Just as the Buddha has attained this, I too shall attain it.
This meaning is explained in detail in the Chapter on Successive Order (*Anukrama-vibhāga*).
The explanation of the successive order is now complete.
The fourth [section], clarifying the boundaries of the stages (*bhūmi*),
has two meanings.
The first is to distinguish the stages with respect to the ten dharmas.
Second, the stages and grounds are distinguished according to the arising of practice.
Regarding the statement that the stages and grounds are distinguished by means of the ten dharmas:
the first two distinguish the principle, which applies universally across the upper and lower levels and is not restricted to the preceding or succeeding stages.
Regarding the latter eight [categories],
there are two meanings for the "entry into characteristics" (*lakṣaṇapraveśa*).

First, in terms of its stage, it is determined to belong to the gateway of the path of non-obstruction (*ānantaryamārga*) at the end of the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*) and prior to the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*).
Second, regarding the practice that extends across the lower and upper stages, the meaning of the observation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) exists both before and upon the stages.
Therefore, the "Chapter on Entering the Stages" states:
"There are four ways of entering the stages."
First, the stage of aspiration and joy;
second, the stage of vision;
third, the stage of cultivation.
The fourth is the stage of culmination (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*).
The fourth [stage] encompasses both the causal and resultant aspects of the stage of skillful means (*upāya-bhūmi*) as well as the third stage.
The fifth is the cultivation of characteristics; the sixth, seventh, and eighth are likewise so designated.
These four superior characteristics pertain to the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
The latter two superior characteristics pertain to the stage of a Buddha (*buddhabhūmi*).
Such is the case regarding the phenomena; as for how they arise in practice, it is as follows:
The first two [teachings] on the superior characteristics produce a mind of understanding;
these belong to the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*).
The latter eight are as previously described.

Furthermore, these ten dharmas are all capable of giving rise to hearing, reflection, cultivation, and realization, as well as the attainment of the fruit; there is no need for further differentiation.
This concludes the fourth section, which clarifies the boundaries of the stages (bhūmi).
Fifth, regarding the distinction between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna,
there are three points.
First, distinguishing their tenets according to their respective stages.
Second, the meaning is distinguished according to practice;
third, the distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles is clarified.
First, regarding the statement "distinguishing the tenets according to their stages":
These ten supreme aspects of the stages are established within the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) to manifest the Great Dharma.
Therefore, the verse from the *Asamasama-āgama-paṭala* states:
"The ten meanings are not seen elsewhere."
This is the cause of bodhi;
this is called the Hīnayāna,
as it serves as a basis for other stages.
By means of this passage, it is proven that the intent of the Master [Zongmi] was to manifest the Great Dharma.
Second, regarding the analysis of the meaning according to practice:
this meaning extends throughout both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
How is this known?
In the second chapter, "The Analysis of the Superior Characteristics," the verse explaining the three natures states:
"Because they do not exist by way of their own essence..."
"Because its own essence does not abide.
The commentary explains:
"This absence of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) regarding the three times applies to both the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna."
This meaning of the "nature of the absence of nature" among the three absences of nature applies to both the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna.
The three absences of nature belong to the gate of the sublation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and their principle is profound;
the establishment of characteristics through the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), however, is shallow in its meaning.
If even profound meanings can be understood through both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles,
how much more so for the Three Natures (trisvabhāva), whose principles are shallow?
Why would they not be understood?
Since those three natures apply to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna categories,
the other nine types likewise apply to both;
thus, their meaning remains unimpaired.
Third, regarding the clarification of the distinctions between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna:
the Hīnayāna distinguishes the principles of reliance and cause-and-effect based on the six consciousnesses,
whereas the Mahāyāna distinguishes the principles of reliance and cause-and-effect based on the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) and so forth.
The Hīnayāna distinguishes the principles of the three natures regarding the presence or absence of defilement and purity solely within the framework of the six consciousnesses;
the Mahāyāna, however, comprehensively distinguishes the differences among the three natures by means of all three consciousnesses.
The Hīnayāna clarifies the meaning of the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*) by means of those six consciousnesses. Therefore,
within the "Chapter on Concentration" (*Samādhipaṭala*) of the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*,
it clarifies that taking the abandonment of emptiness and so forth as objects of cognition within the four formless stages constitutes the meaning of the contemplation of consciousness-only.
The Mahāyāna elucidates the meaning of the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) by means of the three consciousnesses and the true consciousness;
the Hīnayāna distinguishes cause and effect through the śrāvaka’s contemplation of the six perfections and the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*).
The Mahāyāna distinguishes cause and effect based on the Bodhisattva’s six perfections;
the Hīnayāna clarifies the differences in cultivation based on the ten stages of the Hīnayāna;
and the Mahāyāna distinguishes the differences in cultivation based on the Bodhisattva’s ten stages.
The Hīnayāna distinguishes the training in morality (*śīla-śikṣā*) by means of three types of precepts for the śrāvaka:
first, the prātimokṣa precepts;
second, the dhyāna-concomitant precepts (*samādhi-sahaja-śīla*).
Third is that which is conjoined with the Path (*mārga-samprayukta*).
By means of these three types, the distinctions within the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*) are clarified;
alternatively, the distinctions within the training in ethical discipline may also be clarified by way of that category of ethical discipline conjoined with the Path.
In the Mahāyāna, the training in morality (*śīla-śikṣā*) is elucidated through the gateway of the three aggregates of precepts (*tri-saṃvara*).
The first is called the *saṃvara-śīla* (the morality of restraint),
which refers to the ten paths of wholesome action (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*).
The second is called the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*śīla-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*),
which requires the cultivation of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).
The third is called the precept of gathering sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*).
One must practice the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).
As for the Hīnayāna, it distinguishes the training of the mind by means of the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) of the eight dhyāna stages—
namely, the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).
As explained in detail in the "Chapter on Concentration" (*Samādhi-varga*),
the author of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* elucidates the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*) by means of the nine meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
This is as explained in detail in the "Chapter on Dhyāna" (*Dhyāna-varga*).
In the Mahāyāna, the training in concentration is distinguished by means of four meditative absorptions:
first, the Mahāyāna Radiance;
second, the King Who Accumulates Merit.
The third is named Bhadrapāla;
the fourth is named Śūraṃgama,
as explained in detail within the section on the characteristics of training the mind.

In the Hīnayāna, the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*) are distinguished by means of the wisdom of the selflessness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya-prajñā*) and are taken as the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*),
as explained in detail in the "Chapter on Knowledge" (*Jñānapaṭala*).

In the Mahāyāna, the three knowledges (*trijñāna*) are distinguished by means of the wisdom of the non-duality of the self of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-nairātmya-jñāna*) and are taken as the training in wisdom.
As explained in detail within the section on the characteristics of training in wisdom (*prajñāśikṣālakṣaṇa*),
the Hīnayāna defines the fruit of cessation (*nirodhaphala*) by means of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) resulting from the extinction of the countless afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*);
this is as described in the "Chapter on the Noble Ones" (*Āryavarga*).
In the Mahāyāna, the fruit of cessation is distinguished by means of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) that is the non-abiding cessation of the three obstacles,
as explained at length in the section on the characteristics of the fruit of tranquility (śāntiphala).

In the Hīnayāna, the fruit of clear knowledge (vidyāphala) is distinguished within the context of the wisdom of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the wisdom of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) through the gateway of the selflessness of persons (pudgalanairātmya).
In the Mahāyāna, the gates of wisdom and the fruits of wisdom are distinguished by means of the three natures and the gate of suchness-wisdom.
Although there are many ways to differentiate between the great and small vehicles regarding their wisdoms,
this is a rough summary.
The fifth section, the distinction between the Great and the Small, is concluded. Regarding the sixth section, the distinction between Principle and Practice:
the first two [sections] clarify Principle, while the latter eight distinguish Practice.
Since principle is the foundation of practice, it is elucidated first;
since practice is accomplished by relying on principle, the latter eight [perfections] distinguish practice.
Within the first two [of these],...

Because the principle of cause and effect is shallow, the basis is explained first, demonstrating that the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and the sixth and seventh consciousnesses arise from one another and serve as mutual effects.
Because the principle of existence and non-existence is profound, the characteristics of the knowable (*jñeyalakṣaṇa*) are explained second; this should be understood.

Because it distinguishes and determines the meanings of existence and non-existence, as well as the real and the unreal, through the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the "object to be known" (*jñeya*) is explained.
Within the subsequent eight sections explaining practice,
the first six clarify the characteristics of causal cultivation.
The final two [sections] clarify the characteristics of the fruit and its virtuous conduct,
as extensively analyzed previously.
This concludes the detailed analysis of the six principles of practice.
Regarding the seventh [section], the analysis of cause and effect,
there are two meanings.
The first is the analysis according to the ten dharmas.
Second, regarding the classification according to the arising of practice:
as for the statement "classification according to the ten dharmas," the first two characteristics are the dharmas realized through cause and effect, and thus they pertain to both cause and effect.
The causal practices lead to partial realization of the fruits and virtues, while the ultimate realization is reached through the final stage.
Next, six sections clarify the causes,
followed by two sections clarifying the fruits.
This is explained at length as above.
These ten dharmas are thus.
How does one initiate their practice?
If one distinguishes them according to the arising of practice,
all ten give rise to causes;
the first two give rise to the cause of understanding.
The first six give rise to the practice of the cause,
while the final two give rise to the vow of the cause.
Furthermore, these ten dharmas collectively give rise to both cause and effect.
This has been explained in detail as previously analyzed.
The seventh section, the analysis of cause and effect, is concluded.
Eighth, regarding the analysis of the training in the dharmas and the training in conduct:
There are two meanings:
first, the classification according to the ten dharmas that are explained;
second, the classification according to the sentient beings who are to be transformed.
Regarding the analysis of the ten dharmas thus explained:
the first two clarify the dharmas of training (*śikṣā-dharma*),
because they are the dharmas of principle (*nyāya-dharma*).
Therefore, the "Chapter on Peerlessness" states:
the first two [sections] clarify the peerless object;
the subsequent eight clarify the practice of training.
Among these eight, the first six are the causes of training and the latter two are the fruits of training; therefore,
that text states that there are no practices equal to these six, nor any fruits equal to them.
The ten dharmas are thus.
Regarding those to be converted, how is it so?
If one considers the sentient beings who are to be converted:
All ten are dharmas to be studied.
The first two are dharmas of principle;
the subsequent six are dharmas of practice.
Regarding the teachings on the dharmas of the latter two fruits:
when those sentient beings give rise to understanding, practice, and so forth, this is termed "practice.
In the former two [fruits], they give rise to understanding.
Next, six [aspects] give rise to practice;
the final two give rise to aspiration,
as explained extensively above.
The eighth section, the analysis of the training in the dharmas and the training in conduct, is concluded.
Regarding the ninth section, the analysis of the ten dharmas corresponding to the stages (*bhūmi*),
it is measured that this treatise was composed only because its author relied upon the teachings of Maitreya Bodhisattva.
That *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* was spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva;
it is precisely the basis upon which the Bodhisattva Saṃgha composed his treatise.
Therefore, one must differentiate the ten dharmas in relation to it.
As for the ten dharmas:
first, the upholding;
second, the characteristics.
Third, the wings;
fourth, the purification of the mind;
fifth, the abidings.
Six births,
seven inclusions,
and eight stages.
There are nine practices and ten establishments,
as explained in detail in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
However, those ten dharmas take the practice of cultivation alone as their primary theme;
now, these ten [dharmas] universally distinguish both principle and practice.
Furthermore, while those ten dharmas clarify the characteristics of non-retrogression for those who have already attained the stage of spiritual lineage (*gotra*), these clarify it for all stages.
Now these ten characteristics are explained comprehensively from beginning to end;
other meanings are largely the same.
The essence and meaning of these ten supreme characteristics are profound.
This has been explained at length as set forth in the treatise.

For now, I have provided this brief explanation according to the thematic categories. Thus concludes the second section on the Meaning of the Three Consciousnesses in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, extracted from the chapter on the Various Names for the First Superior Characteristic of the Basis.
As for what is called the "three consciousnesses," these are the means by which sentient beings contemplate the Way;
they receive their vital breath and depend upon it in common.
Mysteriously communicating beyond the realm of phenomena,
its meaning encompasses both extremes;
its nature harmonizes the true and the false.
Merit purifies both defilement and purity;
it severs the bonds and the bridge-ford;
it is the sublime path to the fruit of tranquility.
Therefore, the Buddhas have extensively elucidated this meaning within the Tripiṭaka.
Regarding the meaning of the three consciousnesses, there is a detailed analysis in eleven sections.
The first is the explanation of their definitions and meanings.
Second, the discernment of essence and characteristics;
third, the discernment of the true and the false;
fourth, the discernment of delusion and awakening.
1. The fivefold distinction between mind (citta), mentation (manas), and consciousness (vijñāna).
2. The sixfold distinction between the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate. 3.
The threefold distinction according to the three natures (tri-svabhāva).
The eighth [category] subsumes four consciousnesses;
the ninth subsumes eight or nine consciousnesses;
and the tenth subsumes eleven consciousnesses.
Eleventh, the distinction between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
First, regarding the explanation of the names and meanings:
that which discerns the two truths is termed *vijñāna* (consciousness).
There are, in brief, three types of discernment:
first, the ālayavijñāna;
second, the ādānavijñāna.
The third is the arising consciousness.
As for what is called the *ālaya-vijñāna*,
in this context it is correctly translated as the "non-extinguishing consciousness" (*amukta-vijñāna*).
This has two meanings.
First, regarding the gate of the arising and ceasing of consciousness:

it is able to receive pure perfuming and, ultimately, through the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), achieves the merits of the response body (*nirmāṇakāya*); this is called "not perishing."
Second, regarding the gate of the true suchness of consciousness (*vijñāna-tathatā-mukha*):
ultimately, it can be clearly manifested and perfected as the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), which is termed "non-extinction.
Therefore, the *Zhòngmíng zhāng* (Chapter on Various Names) states:
The mundane is not destroyed;
the supramundane is not exhausted.
That which precedes the ten stages of the path is called the mundane.
From the first bhūmi upward, it is termed "transcendent" (lokottara).
According to the chapter on various names in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, there are eight distinct names;
the first is the "seed-consciousness" (bījavijñāna).
This is according to the *Dharmagarbha-sūtra*,
because it can maintain the seeds of both defiled and pure dharmas; thus,
it is called the "appropriating consciousness" (*ādāna-vijñāna*).
This is based on the explanation in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (Sūtra on the Analysis of Sections).
Because it is able to maintain the sense faculties and their seeds,
the third is called the *mūlavijñāna* (root-consciousness).
This is explained according to the Mahāsāṃghika school.
Because it can produce the sixth and seventh [consciousnesses],
and because it can produce both defiled and pure results, it is called the "root consciousness" (mūlavijñāna).
The fourth is called the aggregate that exhausts birth and death (*ātyantika-saṃsāra-skandha*). This is based on the Mahīśāsaka school;
because it remains constantly without ceasing until one reaches *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, it is termed "exhausting birth and death."
The fifth is named ālaya;
its meaning is the same as explained previously.
The sixth is named citta.
Because it possesses manifold meanings and increases [the seeds],
it is called the "retribution-consciousness" (vipākavijñāna) in the seventh [sense];
this is according to the Saṃmitīya school.
Because it arises from the two kinds of seeds— wholesome and unwholesome—
it is called the "consciousness of existence" (*bhavāṅgavijñāna*);
for it acts as the causal branch for those three realms of existence (*tribhava*).
According to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, it has three distinct names.
The first is called the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness),
because it can contain all merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The second is called noble consciousness (*ārya-vijñāna*).
It is that which is realized by noble ones (*ārya*),
for it is that which is employed by those noble ones.
The third is called the consciousness of ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-vijñāna*).
Because it is profound and subtle,
it is designated by three distinct names according to Aśvaghoṣa’s treatise.
First is called True Consciousness,
because the essential nature of consciousness is neither born nor extinguished.
Second is called True Suchness Consciousness.
Because the essence of consciousness is quiescent,
it is called the "Householder Consciousness" (Gṛhastha-vijñāna) and is also called the "Dwelling Consciousness" (Vāsa-vijñāna).
Because defilement and purity share the same basis,

these various consciousnesses can only be fully understood by describing them from the perspective of the gate of the arising and ceasing of consciousness. From the perspective of the gate of the suchness of consciousness, however, [they are not so].
Its essence is the spirit; this is what is meant by "clearly understanding its name.
Second is *ādāna*, which is here named the "appropriating consciousness" (*ādānavijñāna*), because it is able to grasp the fundamental consciousness as the spiritual self (*ātman*).
To grasp that name-and-form as "mine" is called the grasping of consciousness (*vijñāna-graha*).
According to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, it is distinguished into two types.
The first is the grasping consciousness;
its meaning is as explained previously.
The second is called the seven consciousnesses.
It receives its name by way of the six [consciousnesses].
According to the treatise of Aśvaghoṣa, there are seven distinct names:
the first is called "delusive consciousness" (māna-vijñāna).
Because the substance of consciousness is floating and empty,
it is called the second, the consciousness of ignorance;
because it does not comprehend the realm of non-self.
The third is called the karma-consciousness,
because it can defile the ten fetters and give rise to evil karma.
The fourth is called the evolving consciousness.
Because it takes the objects of the self as its cognitive domain,
the fifth is called the manifesting consciousness (*nirbhāsa-vijñāna*);
because it illuminates the objects of the self and manifests one's own mind.
The sixth is called the consciousness of cognition,
because it is able to differentiate the objects of the self.
The seventh is called the consciousness of continuity.
Because self-grasping arises constantly therein,
that stage is called the "accumulating consciousness" (saṃcita-vijñāna) in the sutras;
furthermore, its direct antonym is called the "consciousness of non-understanding" (a-prativedha-vijñāna).
Because it is always associated with the four afflictions,
all the remaining names are translations based on their meaning.
Third, as for its arising:
This has two meanings.
First, it is named after its fruit:
the perfuming of that primary consciousness by the six consciousnesses constitutes its seeds.
Seeds possess two kinds of functional capacities:
the first is the seed of karma,
which is able to produce the two types of fruits— suffering and pleasure.
Second is the seeds of affliction,
which can induce the seeds of karma to bring about rebirth;
from this sense, it is called the "arising consciousness."
Second, it is named according to its cause.
Because this consciousness arises from the seeds of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), it is called the "arising consciousness" (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
This meaning is explained in detail in the chapter on Dependent Origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
According to that *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, there are three distinct names.
The first is called the "arising consciousness" (*pravṛttivijñāna*);
its meaning is as previously explained.
The second is called the *upabhoga-vijñāna* (reception-consciousness),
because it is able to receive the objects of the six sense-fields, such as suffering and pleasure.
The third is called the *ṣaḍ-vijñāna* (six consciousnesses).
Because it arises based on the distinctions of the six sense faculties,
this meaning is explained in detail in the Chapter on Dependent Origination (*Pratītyasamutpāda*).
According to Aśvaghoṣa’s treatise, it is termed the "consciousness of phenomena" (*vastu-vijñāna*).
Because it arises in dependence upon the distinct sense faculties and the six objects,
the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is called the "universally gathering consciousness" (*saṃgrahakavijñāna*) according to that *Laṅkāvatāra*.
Because it is able to receive many objective realms,
the five consciousnesses are called the manifest consciousness (*pratibhāsa-vijñāna*);
because they are able to receive the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).
The first section, the explanation of the names and meanings, is concluded.
Second, in the discernment of the essence,
the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is first discerned.
Next, the seven consciousnesses are distinguished;
subsequently, the evolving consciousnesses are distinguished.
First, regarding the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), there are six sections.
First is the Gate of Comprehending Reality;
second is the Gate of Discerning Reality;
third is the Gate of Comprehending Purity.
The fourth is named the Gate of Distinguishing Purity;
the fifth is named the Gate of Comprehending Coarseness;
the sixth is named the Gate of Distinguishing Coarseness.
Regarding the initial statement on "the gate of subsuming reality":

it means subsuming that pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*) so as to enter into the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), because the pure consciousness is not established [as a separate entity].
As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* by Aśvaghoṣa states:
The non-arising and non-ceasing dharma in conjunction with arising and ceasing is called the ālayavijñāna.
Non-arising is the truth;
arising and ceasing are delusion.
The mutual functioning of these as the fundamental consciousness is termed "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*).
The word "two" serves to exclude the ultimate reality;
it selects the arising and ceasing [of phenomena] to establish them as the gateway to the suchness (*tathatā*) of the fundamental consciousness.
Because it belongs to that pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*).
The *Nirākāra-śāstra* states:
"The signless and the unarisen are precisely the ultimate pure consciousness of Māra."
Regarding "the three encompassing the pure":
within this gate of arising and ceasing, the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) encompasses both the pure and impure categories,
because it is able to sustain the seeds of both the defiled and the pure.
Therefore, the "Chapter on Dependent Origination" states:
"The seeds of good and evil constitute two distinct natures; defilement and purity are likewise twofold.
The seeds of karma and afflictions are termed 'defiled.'"
The seeds perfumed by hearing are termed "pure.
The four words [of the compound] serve to exclude the impure;
that is, they specifically select those [seeds] belonging to saṃsāra.
The four fruits are designated as the pure dharmas (*śukladharma*) because they take the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) as their basis.
However, the perfuming of hearing (*śrutavāsanā*) and so forth belong to the Dharmakāya of another and are not subsumed within the fundamental consciousness.
Therefore, the "Chapter on Supramundane Purity" states:
The permeation of hearing is not subsumed under the nature of the ālayavijñāna; it belongs to the dharmakāya and the vimuktikāya.
Regarding the statement that "the five [aggregates] include the coarse," this means that the fundamental includes the derivative.
The six consciousnesses, the seventh consciousness, and the consciousness of objects are all subsumed within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
Because the fundamental consciousness subsumes them,
the second chapter, "The Analysis of the Superior Characteristics," states:
"One consciousness" refers to the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna).
The sixth and seventh minds are the manifestations (nimitta) of this fundamental consciousness.
The term "sixth" is used to exclude those that are coarse.
Apart from the six and seventh consciousnesses, there exists a fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna).
Therefore, the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* states:
"The term 'manas' designates the first consciousness."
"Mind" (citta) refers to the second consciousness, while "consciousness" (vijñāna) refers to the six consciousnesses.
The Chapter on Impregnation (vāsanā) states:
"The continuity of the perfuming agent is short."
The characteristics of the perfumed continuum have been extensively explained;
this concludes the discernment of the nature of the *mūlavijñāna*. Second, regarding the discernment of the *ādānavijñāna*, there are four sections.
First is named the Gate of Comprehending Reality;
second is named the Gate of Discerning Reality;
third is named the Gate of Following the Source.
The fourth section is the "Simplified Exposition.
First, regarding the "Gate of Encompassing Reality":
arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-non-ceasing together constitute the seven consciousnesses.
Ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is called "real" because it is non-arising;
conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is called "false" because it involves arising and ceasing.
Therefore, the second chapter, "The Superior Characteristics," states:
If the causes of confusion do not exist,
confused consciousness does not arise.
Such factors as the self and sensory objects are what are termed the causes of confusion.
The self-grasping of the seven consciousnesses is termed the essence of confusion.
Within the conventional truth there is the cause of confusion;
within the conventional truth the seven consciousnesses arise.
Ultimate truth is the cause of non-confusion;
in ultimate truth, the seven consciousnesses do not arise.
This is the second section, the gate of distinguishing the ultimate.
The principle of non-arising belongs to the pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*),
whereas the *ādāna*-consciousness with its arising and ceasing belongs to the seven consciousnesses.
Thus, the *Nirākāra-śāstra* states:
The signless and non-arising is called the ultimately pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*).
The mind of arising and ceasing is subsumed under the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Regarding the three statements concerning the fundamental gate:
The seven consciousnesses are subsumed within the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna).
Therefore, the "Chapter on Discrimination" states:
"As for 'one consciousness,' it refers to the one fundamental consciousness."
The sixth, seventh, and second consciousnesses are the manifestations (*nimitta*) of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*);
their substance is the fundamental consciousness itself and possesses no separate substance.
This fourth point distinguishes the fundamental gate.
Apart from the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna), there are separately seven consciousnesses.
Therefore, the "Chapter on Various Names" states:
"The name 'mind' (citta) refers to the second consciousness."
The analysis of the essence and characteristics of the seven consciousnesses is complete.
Next, the six consciousnesses are analyzed through five gates.
First, the gate of subsuming the real.
2. The section distinguishing the true [nature];
3. The section following from the fundamental;
4. The section distinguishing the fundamental.
The fifth is the section on subsuming the fundamental gate.
Regarding the initial statement that it "subsumes the fundamental gate":
it means subsuming that true consciousness (tathatā-vijñāna) into the six consciousnesses.
Arising and ceasing, along with non-arising and non-ceasing, together constitute the six consciousnesses.
Therefore, the "Chapter on Accordance with Principle" states:
"Within the gate of the true suchness of the six sense objects and the ultimate truth, the six sense objects are without marks."
Within the gateway of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) possess characteristics;
it is clearly known that within the gateway of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) are non-arising.
Within the gateway of conventional truth, the six consciousnesses are arising.
Second, regarding the distinction between the provisional and the real:
that which is subsumed under the pure consciousness of non-arising,
and that which is subsumed under the six consciousnesses of arising and ceasing.
As stated in the *Nirākāra-śāstra*,
this has already been analyzed previously.
Third, regarding those who follow the fundamental gate:
As stated in the Chapter on Discrimination,
the above has already been analyzed.
Regarding the fourth point, the "Distinction of the Fundamental Gate" (Simplicity):
As stated in the "Chapter on Various Names," the term "consciousness" refers to the six consciousnesses.
Regarding the fifth section, the "Compendium of the Fundamental Gates":
As explained in the "Chapter on Discrimination," this concludes the analysis of the essential nature as subsumed within the *ālaya-vijñāna* and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Third, regarding the discrimination between the real and the false,
there are three sections.
The first is the discrimination between principle and phenomena.
Second, the analysis according to practice;
third, the analysis according to coarseness and subtlety.
Regarding the first, the analysis according to principle and phenomena:
The limits of arising and ceasing of the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) are termed "delusive";
the limits of suchness (tathatā) are designated as "real.
The same applies to the *ādānavijñāna* and the six consciousnesses.
Therefore, the *Nirākāra-śāstra* states:
"The signless and the non-arising are precisely the *amala*-consciousness, the ultimate pure consciousness.
Arising and ceasing within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) are termed 'delusion'."
The ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is designated as "real.
Thus, the Chapter on Discrimination states:
"Discrimination is without dependence; it is dependently originated and non-arising."
Within the gate of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the seven consciousnesses and the six consciousnesses are of the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), they are called the reality of signlessness (*animitta-tattva*).
Within the gate of conventional truth, the *ālaya-vijñāna* is called the nature of dependence (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
In the ultimate sense, this is called the reality of non-arising.
Having completed the analysis according to the first principle,
the second [analysis] is now conducted according to practice.
The fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and the six consciousnesses (*ṣadvijñāna*) pertain to both the real and the false;
however, *tathatā* (suchness) is exclusively real and does not pertain to the false.
Prior to the first stage (*bhūmi*), when the fundamental consciousness and the six consciousnesses have not yet realized suchness, they are termed "false."
From the first bhūmi upward, the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) within the pure category and the realization of the Dharma-body is termed "True.
Therefore, it is stated in the *Jñāna-prabheda-viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa* (The Distinctive Characteristics of the Differentiation of Wisdom):
"The ālayavijñāna and the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are called the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*)."
This is called the response body (*nirmāṇakāya*),
which serves as the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
This is because within the *ādānavijñāna*, there is no transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) to realize the meaning of true suchness (*tathatā*) through its pure aspects.
Therefore, regarding practice, there is exclusively no truth.
This concludes the second [section], the analysis according to practice.
Third is the analysis according to the coarse and the subtle.
The fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is subtle and permeates both the true and the false.
The sixth and seventh consciousnesses, however, exist only as false and not true while one remains on the stage of ordinary beings.
From the first bhūmi upward, both the fundamental consciousness and the six consciousnesses permeate both the true and the false.
If one reaches the stage of Buddhahood, the original six consciousnesses and the two [manas] are exclusively and solely true.
Therefore, the "Chapter on Discrimination" states:
"The nature of discrimination is non-existent."
Because the sixth and seventh consciousnesses have no substantial reality within the state of ordinary beings, they are called "non-existence" (ākiṃcanya).
Third, the analysis of the true and the delusive is concluded. Fourth, the analysis of understanding and delusion:
There are two approaches:
first, the analysis based on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*;
second, the analysis based on scriptures such as the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.
First, regarding the analysis according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*,
there are three stages.
The first is the analysis based on the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*).
Second, the classification according to the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Third, the classification according to the stage of Buddhahood (*buddhabhūmi*). Regarding the classification according to the stages prior to the [ten] stages, there are three positions.
First is the stage of constant sinking;
second is the stage of the ten faiths;
third is the stage of the nature-ground.
It is constantly submerged within the state [of the ālayavijñāna].
Within the six consciousnesses, it gives rise only to tainted contemplative understanding as well as afflictions and karma;
within the seventh consciousness, it constantly gives rise to the four afflictions and is also able to assist those six consciousnesses in giving rise to both wholesome and unwholesome karma.
Within the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna), it maintains the seeds of contaminated wholesome karma, as well as the seeds of afflictions and unwholesome karma.
How is this known?
As stated in the "Chapter on World-transcending Purity":
From the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) up to the state of enlightenment (*bodhi*),
the functional capacity [of these seeds] is not lost.

By this textual evidence, it is known that ordinary worldlings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*) are constantly submerged [in saṃsāra], possessing only the perfumation (*vāsanā*) of the outflowing wholesome karma of the triple world and unwholesome karma consisting of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Because the cultivation of supramundane goodness has not yet been perfected.
Second, regarding the analysis of the ten stages of faith:
within the six consciousnesses, one is able to give rise to supramundane pure understanding.
Therefore, the "Chapter on World-transcending Purity" states:
"The perfuming of hearing is not a worldly dharma;
it is subsumed under the Dharma-body."
Although the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) of the obstacle of personhood and selfhood (*pudgala-ātman*) have been subdued and eliminated,
the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of the obstacle of dharmas and selfhood (*dharma-ātman*), which consists of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), may still temporarily arise.
Therefore, the "Chapter on Worldly Purity" states:
When the supramundane pure mind has not yet arisen,
these seeds of hearing serve as the antidote to all afflictions of the higher mind;
this is called the stage of the ten understandings (*daśa-vyavakīrṇa-bhūmi*).
The untainted noble path within the stages serves as the supramundane pure mind.
Within the stage of the ten faiths, the seeds of hearing-perfuming serve as the antidote to the active outbursts of the fundamental afflictions of grasping at a self and phenomena.
Furthermore, they can also give rise to contaminated wholesome karma, non-bound karma, as well as unwholesome non-bound karma.
Thus, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, in the chapter on "Abiding," states:
"A Bodhisattva in the stage of practice through understanding may at times give rise to wrong actions of body, speech, and mind, thereby falling into the evil realms."
Even a superior person of the stage of practice through understanding may still give rise to this karma.
One who has attained the lower stage of the ten faiths can discern that there remains residual karma;
this is its unconditioned retribution, which is indeterminate.
If a bodhisattva of gradual enlightenment proceeds from the stage of *śrāvaka* up to that of *pratyekabuddha*,
and then turns their mind toward the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*),

entering the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā-bhūmi*), they likewise possess the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) of the contemplation of the non-existence of self and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-nairātmya*).
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states regarding the initial virtues:
"Those at the stage of Srotāpanna [attain] the aspiration for bodhicitta after eighty thousand kalpas;
up to those at the stage of Pratyekabuddha, who attain the aspiration for Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi after ten thousand kalpas."
From the stage of a srotāpanna up to that of a pratyekabuddha,
they have already departed from the evil destinies within the Hīnayāna;
now they turn back and enter the Mahāyāna.
In the stage of clear knowledge (*vidyā*), which corresponds to the wholesome destinies of the Mahāyāna,
the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) of the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self within the *ādānavijñāna* do not arise at all; rather,
only the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the grasping at a self of phenomena (*dharmātman*) arise.
It can also assist those six consciousnesses in giving rise to out-flowing (sāsrava) wholesome, unwholesome, or non-bound (anivṛtāvyākṛta) karma.
Therefore, the "Chapter on World-transcending Purity" states:
"It is the antidote to all manifest afflictions."
Clear knowledge (*vidyā*) can counteract the sixth and seventh consciousnesses in their active states (*paryavasthāna*).
Although the sixth and seventh are not one, they are termed "all" [in this context].

Within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), there exist two kinds of seeds: the supramundane perfuming of hearing (*śrutavāsanā*) and the seeds of both outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) karma.
Furthermore, there are seeds for the two types of grasping— the grasping at a self of persons and the grasping at a self of phenomena—
and likewise there are the two kinds of non-bondage karma, both wholesome and unwholesome, as well as the fruits of such non-bondage karma;
these may be understood by analogy with what has been stated above.
The analysis of the ten stages of faith is completed.
Third, regarding the analysis of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*):
it is the capacity within the six consciousnesses to give rise to the untainted contemplative understanding of the two kinds of emptiness—of persons and of phenomena.
Within the ten stages of understanding (*daśa-adhimukti-bhūmi*), one gives rise to the understanding of the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*).
From the ten stages of practice (*daśa-caryā*) upward, one gives rise to the contemplative understanding of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
Furthermore, one can give rise to the two types of non-bound karma—wholesome and unwholesome—within contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*).
Furthermore, when experiencing the fruits of non-bondage karma,
the latencies (*anuśaya*) of the grasping at a self and persons also have the sense of arising temporarily,
and the dharmic norms (*dharma-nyāya*) also have the sense of manifesting.
Thus it is known that bodhisattvas prior to the [first] bhūmi attain the realization of the contemplation of selflessness (*anātman*).
This is as explained in the chapter on the distinction between the two types of knowledge for entering the superior characteristics:
they have already thoroughly penetrated the principle of the two kinds of selflessness within the stage of skillful means (*upāya*).
Regarding "expedient means" (*upāya*):
that which precedes the stages (*bhūmi*) is the stage of expedient means;
thus it is known that during the ten levels of understanding (*daśa-adhimukti*), one attains the understanding of the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*).
From the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) upward, one attains the realization of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
The characteristics of all practices within the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*) are the same as those of the preceding lineage (*gotra*);
even if there are slight differences, they are not significant in meaning.

Within the ādāna-vijñāna, there arise only the latent tendencies (anuśaya) for the habitual grasping of a person-self (pudgala-ātman), as well as the manifest afflictions (paryavasthāna) regarding the dharmas.
Within this fundamental consciousness (mūla-vijñāna), there exist the two kinds of seeds of non-outflow (anāsrava-bīja) pertaining to the two forms of selflessness (nairātmya).

Furthermore, there are also the seeds of contaminated wholesome and unwholesome karma, as well as non-bound karma, along with their resultant retributions of suffering, pleasure, and the indeterminate;
these may be understood by analogy with what precedes.
Having completed the analysis according to the stages prior to the [first] ground, next, the second part is the analysis according to the ten grounds.
Within the six consciousnesses, one is able to give rise to the contemplative understanding of the two kinds of selflessness—
of persons and of phenomena. Consequently, the two types of grasping at a person and at phenomena never arise,
nor do the two kinds of outflowing karma— wholesome and unwholesome— nor the non-bound karma.
Within the *ādāna-vijñāna*, neither the habitual tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the person-self (*pudgala-ātman*) nor the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) of dharma-grasping arise.
Furthermore, the six consciousnesses of true permanence partially attain the three bodies (*trikāya*).
Therefore, it is said in the *Ciyin xiuzhong* (The Cultivation of Cause and Effect):
On the first stage, one realizes the meaning of the transcendence of outflows.
Because one realizes *tathatā*, the *dharmakāya* is manifested;
because the pure aspect of the fundamental consciousness undergoes a transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), the *saṃbhogakāya* is established.
Based on the two bodies, the manifestation of activity gives rise to the *nirmāṇakāya*.
Having completed the analysis according to the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the third section is the analysis according to the Buddha stage (*buddhabhūmi*).
Within the six consciousnesses, all contaminated afflictions and karmic actions do not arise at all.
The two types of afflictions associated with giving are also permanently and entirely absent.
Within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), all seeds of the impure categories of afflictions and karma are completely non-existent.
Furthermore, within the six consciousnesses, even the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) has ceased.
The arising and ceasing of the pure aspect of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) also ceases;
being conjoined with original purity, it accomplishes the *saṃbhogakāya*.
Therefore, the "Chapter on World-transcending Purity" states:
When the four virtues are perfected, the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is entirely exhausted.
Because the originally pure [nature] merges with the primordial purity,
it causes the four virtues of primordial purity to be fully manifested.
Within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and among the six consciousnesses, all impure elements and the like are forever transformed, while the pure elements are eternally established.
Therefore, it is said regarding the supreme characteristic of quiescent extinction:
The impure factors are forever transformed, and the pure factors are forever established.
This fundamental nature is called the "transformation of the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
That same text further states:
The fivefold Dharma-body, being stainless and pure, corresponds to the state of Buddhahood without distinction; it is eternally perfected as the original nature.

Furthermore, according to the superior characteristics of the differentiation of wisdom, it is said that the *ālaya-vijñāna* is also called the "arising consciousness" (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and the "enjoyment body" (*saṃbhoga-kāya*).

It is clearly known that the pure factors of the six consciousnesses and the pure seeds of the fundamental consciousness possess the meaning of *āśraya-parāvṛtti* (transformation of the basis) resulting in the *saṃbhogakāya*.
This is termed the *saṃbhogakāya* because it is able to experience the bliss of the pure lands and so forth.
The coarse classification has been thus distinguished based on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
Next, it is distinguished based on the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* and other sūtras;
the remaining meanings are the same as those in the *Saṃgraha*.
Within the ādāna-vijñāna, there are differences between delusion and awakening;
these must be further distinguished.
What is the meaning of this?
To provide a comprehensive explanation based on the underlying meaning:
within the seventh consciousness, there is also the aspect of contemplative understanding (*vipaśyanā*).
Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
The wisdom that slays the seven consciousnesses is called "shedding the blood of the Buddha.
Śrīmālādevī also says:
"Regarding the wisdom of these six consciousnesses and the mental factors..."
It is clearly understood that there is the meaning of contemplative realization.
If one follows the Hīnayāna,

within the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*), one suppresses the active manifestations of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and gives rise to mundane contemplative realization through the force of its habitual tendencies.

Having attained the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*), one severs the seeds of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and gives rise to the realization of untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-darśana*).

Within the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-bhūmi*), the seeds of the active outflows (*paryavasthāna*) of the four afflictions are completely exhausted, and the path of the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) is fulfilled.
Therefore, the "Chapter on Various Names" states:
"Within those who follow the True Dharma, there are three grades.
The first abides in right reflection."
The second is in the stage of correct cultivation;
the third is in the stage of those still in training (śaikṣa).
Of these, the former two have suppressed their view of self.
Third, the view of self is extinguished.
From the stage of patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) upward, one is termed a learner (*śaikṣa*).
According to the Mahāyāna, however:

In the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā-bhūmi*), the bodhisattva of sudden enlightenment suppresses the active outbursts of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) within the seven consciousnesses and cultivates the understanding of impure contemplation (*sāsrava-vipaśyanā*).
As for the bodhisattva of gradual enlightenment, by reaching those ten faiths, they also exhaust the seeds of the four delusions (*catur-kleśa*).

For those who attain sudden enlightenment, from the stage of the Ten Understandings (daśa-vidyā) upward, they cultivate untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-vipaśyanā*) within the seven consciousnesses; they permanently sever the seeds of the four afflictions (*kleśa*) along with their active manifestations, while simultaneously suppressing the grasping at dharmas (*dharma-grāha*).
From the first bhūmi upward, within the seven consciousnesses, one cultivates the realization of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) to sever the seeds of attachment to phenomena;
this reaches its ultimate exhaustion at Buddhahood.
There are no authentic sūtras or śāstras concerning this.
Inferring from this principle, its implication is as follows. Question:
Since the mind of the seven consciousnesses cannot hear the True Dharma, how can it induce the path of remedy and sever all afflictions?
The commentary states:
One should recognize that although the ālayavijñāna does not depend on the six consciousnesses to arise,
this is how we know it to be so.
Although within those seven consciousnesses one has not heard others speak of a false self,
because the six consciousnesses have previously heard of the Path,
those seven consciousnesses can give rise to the defiled category of self-clinging and the pure category.
Although the selflessness [of the person] is not explicitly heard within those seven consciousnesses,
because selflessness has been previously heard within the six consciousnesses,
those seven consciousnesses eventually give rise to the understanding of selflessness.
Furthermore, what is the harm?
The fourth [section], the analysis of delusion and awakening, is concluded.
There are further meanings which shall be analyzed in detail within the section on the meaning of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
Regarding the fifth [section], the discrimination of mind, thought,
and consciousness, there are three gates.
The first is the discrimination according to the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*.
The second [section] analyzes according to the *Tattvasiddhi* (Chengshi lun).
The third analyzes according to the Mahāyāna. Regarding the statement "analyzing according to the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* (Zaxin lun)":
that treatise divides the meaning of its six consciousnesses into three categories.
As stated in the "Chapter on Elements" (Dhātuvarga):
that which arises through accumulation is called *citta*;
that which arises subsequently is called *manas*.
"Discernment" (vijñapti) is the name for consciousness (vijñāna).
In that context, these three meanings are distinguished by way of five gates;
namely, first, the name.
Second, the two meanings;
third, the three karmas;
fourth, the four worlds.
There are five designations.
First, by means of the distinct names, its three meanings are verified;
thus its direction may be known.
Second, the distinction of meaning is revealed through its semantic differentiation,
as explained above.
Third, regarding the term "action" (karma):
To know from afar is the meaning of "mind";
this knowledge pertains to future phenomena.
To know beforehand is the meaning of "meaning" (artha).
This knowledge of past phenomena is the meaning of consciousness as continuous rebirth;
this knowledge of present phenomena is [the meaning of consciousness].
Regarding the fourfold explanation of "world" (*loka*):
that which is past is called "mind" (*manas*),
because "mind" carries the sense of being a faculty (*indriya*).
That which is future is called "mind" (*citta*),
because the essence of mind is yet to be accomplished;
that which is present is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
Because it is able to cognize present objects.
The preceding mention of "activity" clarifies the function of the mind;
the essence of the mind, which currently knows objects of the three periods of time, is termed its activity.
This mention of "worlds" clarifies the essence of the mind;
these three worlds are distinguished by their different names through horizontal classification.
The fifth term, "provisional designation," refers to this.
Within the eighteen elements (dhātus), the designation "mind" (citta) is established;
within the twelve bases (āyatanas), the designation "intellect" (manas) is established;
and among the five aggregates (skandhas), the designation "consciousness" (vijñāna) is established.
In the gateway of the *dhātus*, it is called "mind" (*citta*) with respect to its essence;
in the gateway of the entrances, it is called "intellect" (*manas*) with respect to its characteristics;
and in the gateway of the aggregates, it is designated as "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) with respect to its function.
The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* is thus. Next, regarding the analysis according to the *Tattvasiddhi*, there are two parts.
First, the analysis according to the specific [treatise].
Second, regarding the general classification:
as for the term "regarding the specific," that treatise speaks of four types of mind.
First, consciousness;
second, perception;
third, sensation.
Fourth, the practice of knowing reality through the mind of consciousness,
namely, [discerning] colors such as blue and yellow.
Perception and mind are known to be provisional;
that is to say, they refer to forms such as long and short,
while sensation involves the reception of what is disagreeable or agreeable.
This refers to engaging with objects such as the pleasant and the unpleasant,
which gives rise to wholesome or unwholesome conduct;
that is, it refers to the volitions of body, speech, and so forth.
There are three layers of four types of consciousness.
First, the four types of consciousness of the five sensory cognitions,
which arise based on the present five sense objects.
Second, the four mental states of the five sensory consciousnesses arise based on the past five sense objects.
Third, the four mental states of the sixth mental consciousness [arise from the present].
It arises from conditions such as space and conventional designations.
Within these three layers of the four types of mind,
if one discusses them individually, all take the first layer as being designated by the names "consciousness" (vijñāna), "mind" (citta), and also "intellect" (manas).
The other three are not so; therefore,
the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* establishes a "Chapter on Mental Factors" (*caitasika-varga*),
wherein the first category consists of the mind itself.
The remainder are termed "number.
Second, regarding the general classification:
third, the three—consciousness, mind, and intellect—all may be called "mind" (*citta*), all may be called "intellect" (*manas*), and all may be called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
Therefore, the *Tattvasiddhi* establishes the chapter on "The Absence of Mental Factors" (*acittaka-varga*).
Furthermore, that treatise states:
"That which is able to take an object does so by means of the mind."
The four minds are all able to take [all objects] as their cognitive objects;
this is how it is according to the *Tattvasiddhi*. How is it in the Mahāyāna?
There are also two meanings [to this].
First, the general classification;
second, the specific classification.
Regarding what is called the general classification:
Among the three types of consciousness, the name [ālayavijñāna] possesses these three meanings.
Therefore, in the "Chapter on Synonyms," the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) is named *citta*;
*citta* is called "mind" (*citta*).
Within the chapter on characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the fundamental consciousness is termed the "mind element" (*manodhātu*);
this meaning of "consciousness" is discussed throughout the preceding and following sections.
As for the three meanings of the *ādāna-vijñāna*:
In the chapter on "Various Names," it is called the *kliṣṭamanas* (defiled mind),
because it serves as the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) for the six consciousnesses.
Furthermore, it says:
The Buddha spoke of the name "mind" (*citta*);
this name refers to the second consciousness.
This is called *ādana*.
Because the second consciousness arises by taking the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) as its object and giving rise to the grasping of a self, it is called "mind" (citta).
The meaning of this consciousness is evident and requires no further elaboration.
Regarding the three meanings as distinguished within the six consciousnesses:
In the "Chapter on Various Names," it says:
"First, that which can serve as the sequential condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the arising of that [consciousness]—
the previously ceased consciousness— is the mind (*manas*)."
This takes the mind that has just ceased among the six consciousnesses as the mental faculty (*manas*),
and the subsequently arising mind as consciousness (*vijñāna*);
furthermore, it takes the basis upon which consciousness arises as the mental faculty.
This takes the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) as the mental faculty (manas-indriya).
In the "Chapter on Dependent Origination" (Pratītyasamutpāda), it is termed the "appropriating consciousness" (upabhoga-vijñāna),
because it is capable of experiencing the six sense objects.
Based on this passage, it is proven that the six consciousnesses possess the meaning of "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
Since they are designated as "mind-learnings" (*citta-śikṣā*) within the section on the superior characteristics of the seventh [consciousness],
we know that the six consciousnesses are called "mind" (*citta*).
The general meaning is as explained above.
What is the specific meaning?
The fundamental consciousness is called "manas" (the mind).
Because it is the faculty of mind (manas),
the seven consciousnesses are called "mind" (citta);
for they constantly take the object of the self as their sphere of perception.
The six consciousnesses are called "consciousness" because they cognize the six sense objects. Therefore,
the *Zhongming zhang* (Chapter on Various Names) states:
"Citta" refers to the second consciousness;
"vijñāna" refers to the six consciousnesses;
and "manas" refers to the first consciousness.
The fifth section, the analysis of mind, thought, and consciousness, is concluded.
Regarding the sixth section, the analysis of the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate:
first, the six consciousnesses are distinguished.
Next, the seven consciousnesses are distinguished;
subsequently, the fundamental consciousness is distinguished.
Within the six consciousnesses:
First, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* is examined;
next, the *Tattvasiddhi* is examined;
finally, the Mahāyāna is examined.

According to the tenets of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*, within the stage of the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*), there exists only innate goodness (*upapatti-labdha-kuśala*) and no acquired goodness (*prāyogika-kuśala*);
furthermore, there exist only afflictions abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) and no afflictions abandoned through the vision of the truths (*darśana-heya-kleśa*).

There is only the neutral state born of retribution (*vipākaja-avyākṛta*), with no other three types of neutral states—namely, those of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), deportment (*airyāpathika*), and transformation (*nairmāṇika*).

Within the stage of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna-bhūmi*), both types of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) are present: those acquired by birth (*upapattilābhika*) and those produced through effort (*prāyogika*).
The universal [minds] give rise to both the afflictions of the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.
The four types of neutral [minds] are those born of retribution, those of deportment, those of craftsmanship, and those of transformation;
such is the *Samyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*.
Next, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Chengshi lun) is examined.
The doctrine of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* regarding the threefold nature of the four types of consciousness has been explained above.
Among these four types of consciousness, the first three are all indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Only the fourth mental state, the application of the mind (*citta-prayoga*),
penetrates all three natures (*trisvabhāva*). Because the preceding three mental states each constitute a single moment with distinct objects of perception and lack continuity,
they are conventionally designated as indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
The fourth, the mind of practice, applies to both the provisional and the real, and thus encompasses all three natures.
Therefore, it is as described above.
How is this so in the Mahāyāna?
In the Mahāyāna, all six consciousnesses pervade the three natures;
this is largely the same as in the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*.
Next, the ālayavijñāna is distinguished.
The two treatises of the Hīnayāna do not distinguish *dāna*;
they discuss it only according to the Mahāyāna.
If one relies on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, [it is as follows].
