The *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) is exclusively obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and has no other meaning.
However, according to the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* and other scriptures, it also permeates the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*).

Because it arises simultaneously with the six consciousnesses and the minds of the three natures, acting as an auxiliary to the six consciousnesses in accomplishing wholesome, unwholesome, and other karmas, it possesses the three natures.
The *Dharmadharmatāvibhaṅga* is likewise.
Next, regarding the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*),
even the two treatises of the Hīnayāna do not clarify it.
However, if we distinguish them according to the Mahāyāna,
there are four types therein.
First, distinguishing them based on their inclusion of the ultimate truth.
Second, the analysis from the perspective of the essence of consciousness as subject to arising and ceasing;
third, the analysis from the perspective of its function;
fourth, the analysis from the perspective of time.
Regarding the initial inclusion of the true and the discernment [of the false]:
to recognize the gate of True Suchness (tathatā) is excellent in principle;
to recognize it within the gate of arising and ceasing (utpāda-nirodha) allows its meaning to pervade the three natures (trisvabhāva).
That which maintains wholesome seeds is called wholesome;
that which maintains unwholesome seeds is called unwholesome;
its essential nature is indeterminate.
Second, regarding the analysis of the substance of the arising-and-ceasing consciousness (*utpāda-nirodha-vijñāna*):
from the perspective of its arising from karmic seeds, its substance is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Therefore, the *Prakaraṇapāda* (Chapter on the Differentiation of Phenomena) states:
The ālayavijñāna is unobscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*),
because it is not defiled by afflictions (*kleśa*).
That same text further states:
Because the causes are wholesome or unwholesome, the result is non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

By means of this textual evidence, it is proven that the seeds of wholesome and unwholesome karma within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) belong to the category of retributive indeterminate (*vipākāvyākṛta*).
Third, regarding differentiation by way of function:
because its essence is understood through its function, it is common to all three natures.
From the perspective of being perfumed by the unwholesome, it becomes an unwholesome seed.
From the side of perfuming by the wholesome, wholesome seeds are formed;
from the side of perfuming by the indeterminate [states] of deportment and craftsmanship, indeterminate seeds are formed.
Therefore, the "Chapter on the Impure" states:
This mental consciousness takes the consciousnesses of the three natures as its root;
this is called the fundamental consciousness,
which serves as the basis for the consciousnesses of the three natures.
Because the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) simultaneously relies [upon it],
the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) functions as its primary basis.
Fourth, regarding the analysis by way of time:

The initial perfuming of the two types of karma—wholesome and unwholesome—upon the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) has a subtle similarity to the indeterminate nature (avyākṛta) of that consciousness in its capacity to draw forth results.
Therefore, the "Chapter on Identity and Difference" states:
"Just as when a single thread is woven into a garment, it shares the same white color as the garment."
Later, when the seeds of karma are about to ripen, they are moistened by the assistance of craving and other factors, thereby completing their wholesome or unwholesome nature.

Once bound like cloth and placed into a dye-vat, their appearance differs from the original seed; as the primary cause ceases, the retribution arises and the fruit is established as neutral (*avyākṛta*).
Just as when a garment is untied, its characteristics all become manifest.
This concludes the sixth [section], the analysis of the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
Seventh is the analysis of the three natures.
This refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). This meaning is manifold;
it shall be analyzed in detail in the Chapter on the Three Natures.
For now, let us briefly distinguish between the coarse and the subtle.
The fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is subtle and capable of sustaining both the pure and the defiled; it is therefore termed "dependent nature" (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
The sixth and seventh consciousnesses are coarse and consist of conceptualizing minds; they are termed "imagined nature" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
The non-arising of conceptualization through dependence on others is called the ultimate reality.
This concludes the seventh section, the analysis of the three natures.
Eighth, next follows the analysis summarizing the four consciousnesses.
Regarding the four consciousnesses,
they are explained in detail in the second chapter on the characteristics of the superior marks (*viśiṣṭa-lakṣaṇa*).
The first is called the consciousness resembling the sense organs (*indriya-sadṛśa-vijñāna*).
The first refers to the five faculties, such as the eye;
the second refers to the consciousnesses that resemble objects,
namely the six objects, such as form.
The third is the semblance of my consciousness;
that is to say, the "object-as-me.
The fourth is the semblance of the consciousness-of-consciousness.
This refers to the two minds, the sixth and the seventh.
The meaning of these four consciousnesses shall be analyzed in detail in the chapter on the four consciousnesses.
That which resembles a self-consciousness is the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna).
"Consciousness" refers to the sixth and seventh consciousnesses.
Regarding the statement that they "resemble the faculties and resemble the objects," there are two meanings.
First, the faculties are subsumed under consciousness;
because objects follow consciousness,
they are included within the six consciousnesses.
Second, the derivative follows the fundamental;
that which is subsumed under the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and appears as a self-consciousness is the fundamental consciousness itself.

Regarding that which is subsumed by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and appears as consciousness: in terms of its characteristics, it is comprised within the sixth and seventh [consciousnesses].
As for the ninth [point], which distinguishes the inclusion of the eighth and ninth consciousnesses:
Within this, there are two parts:
first, clarifying the essential nature and characteristics of the eight and nine consciousnesses;
second, the differentiation of faculties and objects. Regarding the statement "the essential nature of the eight and nine consciousnesses":
These two consciousnesses may be called eight consciousnesses or nine consciousnesses; thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
"The various consciousnesses, eight or nine."
In the initial "Chapter on the Characteristics of the Superior," it is also stated:
"Among the eight consciousnesses, any one of them may be perfumed by dharmas of the impure category.
Regarding the phrase "separate from the eight":
Within this, there are two [aspects]:
first, discerning the subtle from the coarse;
second, arising the coarse from the subtle.
Regarding the statement "distinguishing the subtle from the coarse":
within the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), they are divided into six according to their respective sense faculties;
the seventh is the *ādāna-vijñāna*.
Regarding the eighth, the *ālaya-vijñāna*,
the statement "arising from the subtle to the coarse" takes the *ālaya* as the primary [basis].
Dāna is the second.
The section on origination is divided into six;
these together constitute eight.
As stated in the "Chapter on Various Names," regarding the phrase "separated from nine":
the first three consciousnesses are divided into eight within the gate of arising and ceasing.
Because the objects they take as conditions differ,
consciousnesses are unified into one within the gate of True Suchness (tathatā),
due to their commonality in internal illumination.
By including the true suchness (*tathatā*) within consciousness, there are nine [categories] in total.
Thus, the "Chapter on the Signless" in the *Nirākāra-śāstra* states:
"The nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is eternally non-existent."
The dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) also does not exist.
The non-existence of these two is precisely the amala-vijñāna.
Therefore, in the ultimate sense, there is only the single pure consciousness (*amalavijñāna*). Furthermore,
the foreign tradition states that in the "Bodhisattva Chapter" of the *Seventeen Stages Treatise* (*Saptadaśabhūmi-śāstra*), the *amalavijñāna* is extensively analyzed as the ninth consciousness.
The analysis of the essence and characteristics of the eight and nine consciousnesses is concluded. Second, regarding the discrimination of the faculties and objects:
the *ālaya-vijñāna* takes pure consciousness as its faculty, while it also employs the sixth and seventh consciousnesses as its faculties.
Therefore, the "Chapter on Impurity" states:
"This retributive consciousness takes the defiled consciousness as its root.
The two minds—the sixth and seventh—arise with the afflictions of taking birth; these are termed 'defiled' and constitute the root."
It universally takes as its objective sphere phenomena such as existence, non-existence, neither existence nor non-existence, and so forth.
Therefore, the "Chapter on Impurity" states:
"The object-sphere of this retributive consciousness is moreover unknowable."
This is an analysis from the perspective of the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛtti-vijñāna).
The seven consciousnesses primarily rely on the fundamental consciousness (mūla-vijñāna) as their root;
they also rely on the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) among the six consciousnesses as their root.
It relies on purity from afar as its support,
taking that fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) as the object of the self (ātman) and the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) and other dharmas as belonging to the self (ātmīya).
Within the evolving consciousnesses,
if the mental consciousness takes the original seven consciousnesses as its roots,
it means that it relies on the pure consciousness from afar as its supporting root.
If these five consciousnesses take the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) as their root,
they also take the five physical sense organs, such as the eye, as their roots;
they take the six objects, from visible forms up to mental phenomena (dharma), as their objective fields.
If one discusses this in terms of the true suchness (*tathatā*) and pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*) of the three consciousnesses,
the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) are of the same substance and there are no separate dharmas.
Nevertheless, although they are of the same substance, they may still be designated by the conventional terms "sense organs" and "objects."
Taking the mind of true permanence as pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*),
taking the true and eternal *dharmadhātu* as its root,
and taking the realm of *tathatā* as its objects.
The second section on the discrimination of sense bases and objects is concluded.
The tenth section subsumes the eleven consciousnesses.
As for what are called the "eleven consciousnesses":
This is also explained in detail in the "Chapter on Characteristics.
First is the body-consciousness;
[it consists of] the five faculties, such as the eye.
The second is called the "body-consciousness," which refers to the seventh consciousness;
the third is called the "experiencer-consciousness."
This refers to the fundamental consciousness.
Fourth is the "consciousness of what is to be experienced," which refers to the six external objects.
The fifth is called the consciousness of meditative attainment (*samāpatti-vijñāna*),
which refers to the six consciousness elements (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna-dhātu*).
The sixth is called the consciousness of the world (*loka-vijñāna*).
The three periods of time are long-lasting.
The seventh is called the consciousness of enumeration,
which refers to the lateral counting of the infinite.
Eighth, there may be the consciousness of the locus of names and designations (*nāma-vyañjana-vijñapti*) based on the greater or lesser extent of the realm of sentient beings;
that is, the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).
Ninth, there is the consciousness of names and expressions (*nāma-vyavahāra-vijñapti*).
This refers to the consciousness that sees, hears, learns, and knows.
It has the perfuming of these nine types of verbal expression as its cause.
The tenth is called the consciousness of the distinction between self and others.
This refers to the distinction between others and one's own self;
it takes the habitual tendencies of the view of self as its cause,
and it is the consciousness that does not cease throughout the eleven good and evil realms of existence.
This refers to the continuity of the six realms of existence,
which takes the perfuming of the *bhavāṅga* (existence-constituent) as its cause;
this shall be analyzed in detail within the chapter on the eleven consciousnesses.
The second body is subsumed under the *ādāna-vijñāna*;
the third, the experiencer-consciousness (*vedaka-vijñāna*), is subsumed under the *ālaya-vijñāna*;
and the fifth, the consciousness of formal reception (*sampraticchaka-vijñāna*), is subsumed under the six consciousnesses.
First, body-consciousness is subsumed under the five consciousnesses when categorized according to its faculty,
and subsumed under the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) when categorized according to its derivative.
Fourth, the consciousness of what is to be experienced is subsumed under the six consciousnesses when categorized according to its object.
The derivative [consciousnesses] follow from the fundamental, being subsumed within the fundamental consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*).
The worldly enumerations of self and other, as well as the two paths, are collectively subsumed within the three consciousnesses.

The eighth, the locus-consciousness (*sthāna-vijñāna*), takes the objects from the perspective of the consciousness, and thus the four consciousnesses of eye, nose, tongue, and body are subsumed therein.
Because it has the four objects as its substance,
it is subsumed under the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) since the derivative follows the root.
The ninth, the verbalizing consciousness (abhilāpavijñāna), is subsumed under the six consciousnesses.
Because it takes seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing as its essence,
the tenth [section] concludes the subsumption of the eleven consciousnesses.
Regarding the eleventh [section], the distinction between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna:
The name and substance of the six consciousnesses are common to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna,
because these six consciousnesses encompass both the coarse and the subtle;
in their lower states, they are coarse in character.
Regarding the upper [level], the characteristics are subtle.
The names "root consciousness" (mūlavijñāna) and "seven consciousnesses" (saptavijñāna) apply to both the Mahayana and Hinayana;
however, in terms of their meaning, they pertain only to the Mahayana.
Because the meaning of these two consciousnesses is subtle,
it was not explained to the followers of the Hīnayāna as they did not yet understand it.
As for the name "fundamental consciousness" (mūlavijñāna) used by the Hīnayāna:
As explained at length in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (Chapter on Various Names), [the ālayavijñāna] is called "joy," "bliss," "ālaya," and so forth.
Regarding the naming of the seven consciousnesses,
as stated in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, the nature of the ear is called ignorance (*avidyā*) and is also called the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), and so on.
The three natures and the mind are all similar to the seven consciousnesses and four delusions of the Mahāyāna.
This concludes the eleventh section on the distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles.
The meaning of the three consciousnesses is extensive; this brief summary is sufficient for now.
Chapter Three: The Meaning of the Four Afflictions. This appears in the section on "Various Names" within the chapter on "The Superior Characteristics of the Basis.
Regarding the so-called four afflictions:
they are the very source of the mass of defilements.
Defilements and fetters share a common basis;
wishing to cause those who aspire to the Way to realize the truth and penetrate the conventional so that the clouds of inversion and delusion may disperse,
the Bodhisattva has extensively elucidated this meaning within the Tripiṭaka.

The Analysis of the Meaning of the Four Delusions in Eleven Sections: 1. Explaining the Names and Discerning the Essence; 2. Analysis by Way of Objects; 3. Analysis by Way of the Three Consciousnesses; 4. Analysis of Priority and Sequence; 5. Analysis of the Two Obstructions; 6. Analysis of the Three Obstructions; 7. Analysis of the Five Abodes; 8. Analysis of the Six Defilements; 9. Analysis of the Eight Falsehoods; 10. Analysis of the Ten Ignorances; 11. The Limits of Treatment and Severance.

In the initial section on explaining the names and discerning the essence, there are four gates: first, explaining the meaning of the names; second, discerning the essential nature; third, analysis according to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*); and fourth, analysis according to the three realms (*tridhātu*). Regarding the first, the explanation of the meaning of the names:
When the conscious mind is deluded regarding principle, it is termed "confusion.
This confusion is of four distinct types:
the first is called the view of self (ātma-dṛṣṭi).
The second is called self-conceit;
the third, self-love;
and the fourth, ignorance.
Although there are four types of delusion, there are two ways in which they are named.
The first three delusions are named according to what they establish;
the fourth, ignorance (*avidyā*), is named according to its own essential nature.
It may also be named according to that which is deluded;
since the fundamental consciousness is established as the self,
the first three afflictions are named after that which is so established.
Because its substance lacks the clarity of wisdom,
the fourth type establishes its own essence as a scale;
calculating the sovereign primary consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) to be the presiding deity, it is termed the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
Relying on oneself with arrogance is called "self-conceit" (asmimāna).
Clinging to the self is called "self-love" (ātmasneha).
Being deluded regarding the principle of non-self is called "ignorance" (avidyā).
Furthermore, the first three delusions may be named according to what they establish:
because they establish what is non-self as self.
The fourth type is named according to what it is deluded about.
Because they are deluded regarding the principle of selflessness,
the explanation of the definitions and meanings is concluded.
Second, the discernment of the essential nature:
All four afflictions take *ādāna* as their essence.
Within the *ādāna-vijñāna*, erroneously grasping the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) as a sovereign self constitutes the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
Relying on oneself with self-exaltation is called "self-conceit" (asmimāna).
Coveting and cherishing the self is called "self-love" (ātmasneha).
Being deluded regarding the principle of non-self is called "ignorance" (avidyā).
Furthermore, because it is the view of self (ātmadṛṣṭi), it is infinite;
as a false delusion, it consists of four views;
and because it clings to certainty, it is free from doubt.
Because they love me, there is no anger.
This concludes the analysis of their essential nature. Third, regarding the classification according to the three natures:
the essence of the four afflictions is obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta).
Therefore, the "Chapter on Various Names" states:
Because it is defiled, it is of the nature of obscured-neutral (nivṛtāvyākṛta).
It can coexist with the minds of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) of the three natures (trividha-svabhāva).
The term "obscured" (*nivṛta*) carries two meanings:
first, it is called "obscured" because it is covered by the subtle mind of *ālayavijñāna*;
second, it is called "obscured" because it can obscure the understanding of non-self (*anātman*).
That which does not act as a retributive cause to draw forth and accumulate the fruits of suffering is termed "indeterminate" (avyākṛta).

This meaning is similar to that found in the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* regarding the afflictions of the two upper realms, as well as the view of self and the view of extremes within the desire realm.
The classification of the three natures is concluded. Fourth, regarding the classification of the three realms:
the four afflictions do not separately bind the segmented [realms] of the three realms;

rather, they are associated with the afflictions of both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation within the six consciousnesses of ordinary beings amidst the three realms, thereby binding them through defilement.
Therefore, the "Chapter on Various Names" states:
"This consciousness is the basis for the other afflicted consciousnesses;
those six consciousnesses give rise to the two types of delusion—those abandoned through insight and those abandoned through cultivation."
The consciousnesses of the remaining afflictions all take the seven consciousnesses as their basis for the root of defilement.
As it says in the *Vyākhyā*:
"This defiled consciousness arises based upon the first consciousness."
By means of the second consciousness being defiled,
the fundamental consciousness is the first and the seven consciousnesses are the second.
The fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) serves as the primary root,
because it contains the seeds of the ten proclivities (anuśaya).
The seven [evolving] consciousnesses serve as the conditional roots.
Because the seeds of the ten afflictions (*daśa-ānuśaya*) are absent,
it is merely the four delusions that simultaneously defile and bind the contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) of the three realms;
prior to hearing and reflection, these four delusions have not yet been suppressed or extinguished.
Since then, it has always been held that the seventh and second consciousnesses serve as the mental faculty (manas-indriya).
The four afflictions simultaneously defile and bind the ten latent tendencies (anuśaya), causing them to become active afflictions (kleśa) capable of obstructing noble realization.
Defilement causes unwholesome karma, such as volitional action, to draw forth the fruit of suffering;
it defiles wholesome karma, rendering it outflow-tainted (sāsrava) and causing it to draw forth the pleasures of the three realms;
and it defiles neutral phenomena, preventing one from seeing the truth.
Therefore, the "Chapter on Various Names" states that it exists throughout the minds of the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral;
its characteristics are similar to those of the "nature-aggregate ignorance" (*sāmagrī-avidyā*) in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.
However, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* maintains that the ignorance of grasping (*upādāna*) resides in the six consciousnesses because it does not recognize the *ālayavijñāna*.
In this treatise, the four afflictions reside in the seventh consciousness.
The first section, explaining the names and defining the essential nature, is concluded.

The second section, the analysis according to objects, contains four gates: the five aggregates (skandhas), the twelve bases (āyatanas), [the eighteen elements (dhātus), and the twenty-two faculties (indriyas)].
Regarding the thirty-eight realms and the forty-two conditions,
the first point concerning the analysis of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) is as follows:
within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), one reckons the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) characterized by arising and ceasing to be the self (*ātman*).
One reckons the remaining aggregates and the remaining consciousnesses as "mine.
Therefore, the *Ṣaḍdhātuvibhaṅga-śāstra* states:
"One should seek liberation within the ālayavijñāna and the ādānavijñāna."
Thus, they seek liberation within the notions of "self" and "what belongs to the self," conceiving the ālayavijñāna as the self and the seven consciousnesses and so forth as that which belongs to it.
If one knows that the ālayavijñāna is not the self and that the ādānavijñāna and the others are not "mine," one immediately attains liberation.
Furthermore, the five aggregates have from the very beginning been called the ālaya;
yet, they are mutually conceptualized as the self and as what belongs to the self.
Thus, the *Sanghabhedavastu* (Hence-Phase Chapter) states:

"As for body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*), the body consisting of the five sense organs is also the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*). Second, regarding the analysis according to the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*):
among the twelve bases, one reckons the fundamental consciousness within the mind-base (*manāyatana*) as the divine self (*ātman*).
The remaining eleven bases (*āyatana*) are considered "mine.
Furthermore, by subsuming the derivative from the fundamental, all twelve bases are the root consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
These are mutually reckoned as "self" and "mine," and so forth. Regarding the analysis of the thirty-eight elements (*dhātu*):
Within the reckoned eighteen elements (*dhātu*), they take the fundamental consciousness and the mental faculty element (*manas-indriya-dhātu*) to be the self (*ātman*).

They reckon the remaining elements and the remaining consciousnesses to be "self" and "what belongs to the self" (*ātmīya*). Regarding the forty-twofold analysis of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*):
Within the twelve links of dependent origination, one calculates the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*)— the link of consciousness and the link of birth— to be the self,
while regarding the remaining links as "mine. Alternatively,
by subsuming the derivative from the fundamental, all twelve links of dependent origination are the fundamental consciousness itself.
They alternately conceive of these as "self" and "mine," and so forth.
According to the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*, Chapter on Reality (*Tattvapariccheda*),
one conceives of a self with respect to ten phenomena.
These four have been cited;
the remaining twenty-two faculties and so forth may be understood by analogy.
The second section, concerning the classification according to objects, is concluded.

Third, regarding the analysis according to the three consciousnesses, there are three sections: first, clarifying the meaning of their actual arising; second, clarifying the meaning of defiled bondage; and third, clarifying the meaning of the perfuming that forms seeds. As for the "three consciousnesses":
Regarding the arising of the *ādāna-vijñāna* and the *mūla-vijñāna*:
the initial meaning of "arising" (*samudācāra*) resides in the *ādāna*.
Because these four share the same basis as the seven consciousnesses.
Regarding the meaning of the term "defiled bondage," it refers generally to the binding of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).

In ordinary beings, prior to the stage of wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), within the minds of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the *ādāna-vijñāna* constantly arises and binds the afflicted *manovijñāna*, causing it to become outflowing (*sāsrava*).
This has been fully analyzed above in the first section.
Third, regarding the discrimination of perfuming seeds:
the four active afflictions reside in the seven consciousnesses;
they arise in conjunction with the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna).
The perfuming of the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) establishes four seeds;
furthermore, it can defile those six consciousnesses and the ten proclivities (anuśaya),
perfuming the fundamental consciousness so as to bring about the seeds of the ten proclivities and so forth.
However, because the defiled dharmas are weak and inferior,
the six consciousnesses and the ten proclivities must rely on the seeds of the fundamental consciousness as their primary root;
with the four delusions of the seventh consciousness serving as the secondary root, the ten proclivities then arise.
Because the power of supramundane pure dharmas is so strong,
even the seeds of the pure lineage within the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) alone can manifest.
This concludes the analysis of the three consciousnesses.

Regarding the fourth [section], the analysis of priority and sequence, there are three gates: first, the distinct timing of the four afflictions; second, clarifying the distinct timing of the three afflictions while the meaning of ignorance (*avidyā*) is pervasive; third, the simultaneous occurrence of the four afflictions. First, concerning the distinct timing of the four afflictions:
First, ignorance arises, which is deluded regarding the principle of non-self.
Next, the view of self arises, which conceives the fundamental consciousness as a self.
Following that, craving for self arises, which cherishes and clings to the self.
Next, the conceit of "I" (asmimāna) arises, whereby one relies on the self and treats others with contempt.
Thus, the *Zhongming zhang* states:
"Because one does not understand the meaning of non-self, the grasping at a self (ātma-grāha) arises."

From self-grasping arise self-love and self-conceit. Second, regarding the meaning of ignorance as being common to the distinct times of the three afflictions, the *Vibhaṅga* (Chapter on Analysis) states:
"The view of a self is the grasping of a self-mind."
Following the arising of this mind, *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am") arises;
because of *asmimāna*, craving for a self (*ātmatṛṣṇā*) arises.
Therefore, these three afflictions occur at distinct times.
These three delusions all universally take ignorance (*avidyā*) as their cause.
This clearly shows that the meaning of ignorance pervades the three delusions and possesses no separate essence of its own.
Furthermore, it may be that prior to each of the three delusions, ignorance first arises, followed by the arising of the respective delusion.
Therefore, it is said that the three delusions universally take ignorance as their cause. Regarding the statement that the four delusions are simultaneous and of the same substance:
although the four delusions are simultaneous and of the same substance, they are distinguished as four delusions because their functional meanings differ.
The deluded mind of the seven consciousnesses that fails to comprehend the principle of non-self is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
To reckon the fundamental consciousness as the self is called the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), which is also termed self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*).
To rely upon this self and look down upon others is called self-conceit (*asmimāna*).
Covetous attachment to the self is called "self-love" (ātmasneha).
Therefore, although the four afflictions are simultaneous and of the same substance, they are distinguished as four afflictions.
Thus, the *Zhòngmíng zhāng* (Chapter on Various Names) states:
The ignorance that is called "acting alone" (*ekākinī avidyā*) is also called "acting constantly" (*nitya-pravṛttā*).
It is designated as "acting alone" and "acting constantly" because it coexists with those six consciousnesses and with minds of the three natures.
Examining this passage, it is proven that it is not merely ignorance that acts alone.
The view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), the conceit of self (*ātma-māna*), and self-love (*ātma-sneha*) all proceed independently.
Because one does not understand the scope of the meaning of non-self (*anātman*), this is called independent ignorance (*avidyā*) and "always-proceeding" [ignorance].
Regarding the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as the self: from the perspective of the object of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), the view of self operates independently;
from the perspective of the pride that relies on the self to look down upon others, the pride of self (*asmimāna*) operates independently;
and from the perspective of the attachment to cherishing the self, the love of self (*ātmasneha*) operates independently.
All four are always active;
however, because the text is concise, it speaks only of ignorance as acting alone (*ekavartin*).
To say it acts alone does not mean that it arises without being concurrent with the other three types of afflictions among those associated with *ālayavijñāna*.

This clarifies that among the seven consciousnesses, ignorance (avidyā) is called "independent" (ekavartika) because it does not function with a separate entity alongside the ten proclivities (anuśaya) within those seven consciousnesses.
If one considers the six consciousnesses, the ten proclivities also function alongside separate consciousnesses.
However, those that do not function in common consensus are termed "acting alone" (*ekavṛtti*).
Although there are three meanings [for this], they share the same substance and occur simultaneously; thus, the four afflictions are distinguished in their functions.
This interpretation is most excellent.
The fourth section, concerning the sequential distinction, is concluded.

Regarding the fifth section, the distinction based on the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), there are three gates: first, explaining the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*); second, explaining the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); and third, explaining the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). As for the "two obstacles," they have two names.
Based on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, these are termed the obstacle of the self of persons (*pudgala-ātman-āvaraṇa*) and the obstacle of the self of phenomena (*dharma-ātman-āvaraṇa*).
Based on the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, they are termed the afflictive obstacle (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
By means of these two obstacles, the three preceding sections are explained. First, regarding the term "higher mind" (*adhimukti-citta*):
The manifestation of the four afflictions resides in the seven consciousnesses.
In relation to these four afflictions, [the ego-grasping] is invariably subsumed under the obstacle of the person (pudgala-āvaraṇa);
it is also termed the obstacle of affliction (kleśa-āvaraṇa).
Furthermore, the four afflictions may arise simultaneously with the dharma-grasping within those six consciousnesses;
this defiled and bound dharma-grasping is also termed the "obstruction of dharma-self. Second, regarding the term "latent tendencies" (anuśaya):

Among the four afflictions within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), the seeds of the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) are exclusively subsumed under the obstacle of the person-self (*pudgala-ātman*).
Therefore, the *Nirākāra-śāstra* states:

"The latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the manifest outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) are abandoned by the noble understanding of the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) in the Hīnayāna. Regarding the three types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*):

The residual traces of the seeds of these four afflictions are also called the obstacle of the self of persons (pudgala-ātman-āvaraṇa) and the obstacle of the self of phenomena (dharma-ātman-āvaraṇa).
Because they are the residual traces of the obstacle of the self of persons, they are specifically termed the obstacle of the self of persons.
Because it is severed simultaneously with the obstacle of the self of dharmas (*dharmātmagraha-āvaraṇa*), it is also called the obstacle of the self of dharmas.
Thus, the *Nirākāra-śāstra* states:
"The habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are not extinguished by Arhats."
Only by attaining the wisdom that accords with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā-jñāna) can one gradually eliminate [the afflictions].
This wisdom that accords with the nature of phenomena is attained throughout the ten stages of the path of cultivation (bhūmi).
The fifth section, concerning the differentiation of the two obstacles, is now concluded.

The sixth section, which distinguishes [the afflictions] by way of the three obstacles (*trividha-āvaraṇa*), has two parts: first, clarifying the essential nature and characteristics of the three obstacles; second, distinguishing them according to the four delusions (*catur-kleśa*). Regarding the first point, the three obstacles have four meanings.
1. A general discussion of the two obstacles;
2. A separate explanation of the two obstacles;
3. A combined explanation of the two obstacles.
Fourth, the classification according to the stages (*bhūmi*).
Regarding the initial statement that the two obstacles are explained together,

this is based on what is analyzed in the "Chapter on Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-paṭala*) of the first chapter, "The Distinction of the Superior Characteristics of the Basis" (*āśraya-viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
The afflictions of the realization of the truths (satyadarśana-heya) in the Hīnayāna are called "fleshly" afflictions because they are coarse.
The afflictions of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga-heya) in the Hīnayāna are called "skin" afflictions.
Because it is coarse,
the Mahāyāna refers to the stage of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) as a "mental affliction" (*citta-kleśa*).
Thus, that treatise states:
Discriminating internal phenomena while subverting correct principle and establishing what is irrational is called "fleshly affliction.
Discriminating external objects to give rise to delusions such as desire and hatred is called "skin-like affliction.
Discriminating supramundane phenomena is called "mental affliction."
Regarding the second point, the separate explanation of the two obstacles,
it is based on what is taught in the "Chapter on Abiding" (*Vihāra-paṭala*) of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*.
Within the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), there are three grades.
The first is called the afflictions of the higher-middle evil destinies;
they are abandoned at the final moment of the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*), at which point one attains the Dwelling of Joy (*pramuditā-vihāra*).
The second is called all afflictions.
One does not enter the eighth stage by exhausting [defilements] at the seventh stage;
this is called the third [type of] habituation of all afflictions.
One enters the Tathāgata stage by exhausting them at the tenth stage.
The cognitive obstructions are of three grades:
namely, skin, flesh, and bone.
By severing the skin, one enters the first stage (bhūmi).
Cutting through the skin, one enters the eighth stage;
cutting through the bone, one enters the Buddha-stage.
Regarding the three statements that speak of the two obstacles together:
According to the "Chapter on the Distinctions of Practice during the Period of Cultivation" in the fifth [chapter] of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*,
one great kalpa of asaṃkhyeya eons prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) is for the severing of the "outer skin" afflictions.
From the first stage to the seventh stage, during the second great asaṃkhyeya kalpa, one abandons the afflictions of the flesh.
From the eighth stage to the tenth stage, during the third great asaṃkhyeya kalpa, one abandons the afflictions of the mind.
Regarding the fourfold classification according to the stages (*bhūmi*),
as explained in the "Chapter on Cultivation":
prior to the stages, one establishes three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas of faithful practice, diligence, and progressive advancement.
Each of the ten stages is established as thirty-three asaṃkhyeyas.
Within the eleventh stage, the abandonment of the "skin-delusion" establishes the first asaṃkhyeya;
the abandonment of the "flesh" establishes the second.
Because the third [stage] is established upon the abandonment of the mind, there are thirty-three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
The explanation of the essence and characteristics of the three obstacles is complete. Second, regarding the classification according to the four delusions:
Next, regarding the four types of obstacles previously mentioned, the four afflictions are distinguished.
In the first section, the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the Hīnayāna are defiled by the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of self-love among the four afflictions.
In the Hīnayāna, the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are defiled by the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and so forth among the four afflictions;
in the Mahāyāna, ignorance (*avidyā*) consists of the residual habits of these four afflictions.
Second, regarding the separate explanation of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*):
Among the three categories of afflictions,
the first— the category of predominant afflictions leading to the evil destinies—
consists of four types of active delusions present in the stage of perpetual submersion.
Within the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā-bhūmi*), there exist the seeds of the four delusions (*catur-kleśa*).
Above the stage of the ten understandings (*daśa-adhimukti*), there remain the residual habits (*vāsanā*) of the four delusions.
From the second stage, the first *bhūmi*, and above, all afflictions (*kleśa*) are partially eliminated.
In the third [category], from the eighth stage upward, all afflictions and habitual tendencies possess the residual traces of the four delusions (*catur-kleśa*).

Regarding the three grades of cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), only the *avidyā-vāsabhūmi* (ground of the dwelling of ignorance) is identified, without further distinguishing the meaning of those four delusions.
Because it is subsumed under the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*),
the third [point] explains the two hindrances together;
the fourth distinguishes them according to the stages (*bhūmi*).
The meaning of the preceding two sections may be understood by analogy.
The sixth section concludes the analysis based on the three obstructions.

Regarding the seventh section, the analysis based on the five stages (*pañca-vihāra*), there are two parts: first, the elucidation of the essential nature and characteristics of the five stages; second, the analysis in relation to the four delusions (*catur-kleśa*). First, concerning the elucidation of the essential nature and characteristics of the five stages:
The five abiding stages of delusion (*pañca-vāsabhūmi-kleśa*) are explained in detail in the "Chapter on the One Vehicle" of the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*.
The first is the stage of abiding in views (*dṛṣṭi-vāsabhūmi*),
which refers to the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) by followers of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
The second is called the ground of abiding in desire-attachment;
it refers to the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation within the desire realm by followers of the Lesser Vehicle.
The third is called the ground of abiding in form-attachment.
These are the afflictions of the form realm cultivated by followers of the Hīnayāna;
the fourth is called the ground of abiding in craving for existence (*bhavarāga*).
These are the afflictions of the formless realm cultivated by followers of the Hīnayāna.
Furthermore, the three abodes of craving pertain to both the paths of seeing and cultivation;
the fifth is called the abode of ignorance,
which constitutes the afflictions of seeing and cultivation for followers of the Mahāyāna.
Among the six consciousnesses, these are termed "arising delusions";
the seeds of the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) are termed "ground delusions";
and the afflictions of the seventh consciousness are both ground and arising.
Among those six consciousnesses, the delusions [of the sixth] and the four delusions of the seventh consciousness are termed "ground" (*bhūmi*),
because they serve as the root for them.
In relation to the delusive seeds of that fundamental consciousness, the four delusions of the seventh consciousness are termed "arising delusion."

Having finished the analysis of the essence and characteristics of the afflictions of the five dwelling stages by way of the seven consciousnesses above, the second section is the analysis according to the four delusions.
If we consider the four delusions from the perspective of distinct moments:
The four afflictions and the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) of the Śrāvakas serve as the roots of defilement for those [afflictions] and are also termed "afflictions of views.

The three types—self-love (*ātmasneha*), self-conceit (*asmimāna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*), together with their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*)—serve as the roots of defilement common to both the afflictions of views and the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-kleśa*), and are also termed "afflictions of cultivation."
The residual habits of the four afflictions reside in the stage of ignorance (*avidyā-bhūmi*).
If one considers these four afflictions as being simultaneous,
all four serve as the roots for both the afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) and those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
They are also called afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-kleśa*).
The seventh [section] concludes the analysis based on the five abiding stages of affliction (*pañca-vāsabhūmi-kleśa*).
Regarding the eighth [section], which analyzes based on the six types of defilement (*ṣaḍ-rāga*), there are two gates.
First, the essential characteristics of the six defilements are clarified;
second, they are analyzed in relation to the four delusions. Regarding the first, the analysis of the essential characteristics of the six defilements is found in the *Awakening of Faith*.
The first is called the defilement associated with grasping (*grahaṇa-saṃprayukta-kleśa*),
which is severed and exhausted upon reaching the stages of the Two Vehicles up to the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) of the Mahāyāna.
The second is called the defilement associated with non-interruption (*anuccheda-saṃprayukta-kleśa*).
According to the Mahāyāna, it can be completely severed from the stage of the ten faiths up to the stage of the pure mind;
this is called the third type, the defilement associated with conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa-saṃprayukta-kleśa*).
It is severed and exhausted from the second stage up to the seventh stage.
The fourth is called the defilement dissociated from the manifestation of form;
it is exhausted only through the stage of mastery over the eighth form-base.
The fifth is called the defilement dissociated from the mind that is capable of seeing.
It is abandoned through the method of exhaustion by means of the ninth mind, the stage of mastery;
this is called the sixth, the defilement dissociated from the fundamental karma.
It is abandoned through the tenth stage and one enters the Tathāgata stage.
The analysis of the essence and characteristics of the six defilements is complete. Second, regarding the classification according to the four delusions:

the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of these four delusions are subsumed under the first [defilement], the "affliction associated with grasping" (*saṃprayukta-kleśa*).
The residual traces of the four delusions are subsumed within the latter five defilements.
The eighth [section], concerning the analysis of the six defilements, is concluded.

Regarding the ninth [section], which analyzes the eight false discriminations, there are two gates: first, the discernment of the essential nature and characteristics of the eight false discriminations; second, the analysis by way of the four delusions. First, as for the discernment of the characteristics of the eight false discriminations:
As explained in detail in the "Chapter on the Meaning of Reality" (*Tattvārtha-paṭala*) of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*,
there is first that which is called "intrinsic false imagination," which grasps the essence of all phenomena.
The second is called the delusion of differentiation,
which grasps at the conceptualization of all phenomena.
The third is called the delusion of the collection of grasping seeds.
Taking the activity of the supreme dharma:
the first three are attachments to dharmas;
the fourth is the deluded conception of a self.
Grasping at the essence of self and others is the fifth,
the false imagination of "mine," which grasps at what belongs to self and others.
These two are attachments to a person.
The sixth is called the delusion of recollection;
it grasps at favorable objects.
The seventh is called the false discrimination of non-recollection,
which takes as its object a contrary state.
The eighth is called the false discrimination of mutual contradiction.
Taking the middle-range object:
among the eight [stages], the first three are the ground of abiding in ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*);
the next two are the ground of abiding in views regarding a single locus (*dṛṣṭi-ekadeśa-vāsabhūmi*).
The latter three are the ground of abiding for the three types of craving.
Having completed the analysis of the essential characteristics of the eight delusions, the second section concerns the fourfold classification:
the first three delusions are attachments to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) and are not subsumed under the four afflictions.
The two kinds of false conceptualization—“I” and “mine”—are subsumed under the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) among the four afflictions.
The false conceptualization of mindfulness is subsumed under self-love (*ātma-sneha*).
The false conceptualization of non-mindfulness is subsumed under self-pride (*ātma-māna*).
The delusion that contradicts both is subsumed under ignorance (*avidyā*).
The residual habits of the four afflictions are subsumed under the first three [of the eight delusions].
Thus concludes the ninth section, which analyzes the eight types of delusive conceptualization.
The tenth section, which analyzes ignorance through ten types, has two parts:
first, distinguishing the essential characteristics of the ten types of ignorance; second, analyzing them in relation to the four afflictions. First, distinguishing the ten types of ignorance:
According to what is explained in the fifth chapter on the "Superior Antidotes," the first is called the ignorance of the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva-avidyā*);
it is the seed of the clinging to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).
The second is the ignorance that gives rise to wrong conduct toward sentient beings based on bodily actions and so forth.
The third is the ignorance of mental sluggishness and suffering,
which is the ignorance of losing track of what has been heard, reflected upon, and cultivated.
The fourth is called the ignorance that arises together with the view of a self-identity and other subtle afflictive tendencies;
the fifth is called the ignorance regarding parinirvāṇa in the Lesser Vehicle;
the sixth is called the ignorance of coarse characteristics.
The seventh is the ignorance of subtle characteristic-activity;
the eighth is the ignorance of applying effort toward ignorance;
the ninth is the ignorance of not acting out of spontaneous effort for the benefit of sentient beings.
The tenth is the ignorance that lacks mastery over the various dharmas.
These ten types of ignorance are all seeds of the clinging to phenomena (dharma-grāha) within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*).

They also include the residual habits of the ten afflictions (*daśa-kleśa*) within the obstacle of the clinging to a self (*pudgala-grāha*), as well as the residual habits of the seeds of the four delusions.
The first, ignorance (*avidyā*), is named according to its own essential nature.
The subsequent nine types are named in relation to the path of preparatory application (*prayoga*) that they obstruct;
for the arousal of wrong conduct and so forth are all [obstacles to] the preparatory application of the pure category (*śukla-pakṣa*).
These arise from the seeds of hearing, reflection, and cultivation within the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*);
they do not arise from the seed of ignorance (*avidyā*) within the fundamental consciousness.
Furthermore, the twenty-two types of ignorance mentioned below are likewise seeds of the clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) within the fundamental consciousness.
As well as the residual seeds of the habitual tendencies of the grasping at a self and persons,
these are not manifest states;
other cases may be understood by analogy with this.
First, the explanation of the essence and characteristics of the ten types of ignorance is completed. Second, regarding the classification according to the four afflictions:

the active manifestations (*paryavasthāna*) and the latent seeds (*anuśaya*) of these four afflictions are not subsumed under those ten ignorances, nor are they subsumed under the twenty-two ignorances.
The residual habitual tendencies of the seeds of the four afflictions are subsumed under those ten types of ignorance and the twenty-two types of ignorance.
This concludes the detailed classification of the tenth [ignorance] according to the ten types of ignorance.
The eleventh section, on the limits of cultivation and abandonment, has two parts:
first, distinguishing the greatness from the smallness regarding the limits of abandonment for those of the Two Vehicles;
second, clarifying the limits of cultivation and abandonment in the Mahāyāna. Regarding the first, the distinction between the great and the small:
First, the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* is distinguished;
next, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* is distinguished as to why it is so named.
Regarding the distinction of the Lesser Vehicle within the Great [Vehicle]:
This is truly because within the teachings of the Hīnayāna, the seven consciousnesses and the four afflictions were not yet distinguished;
now, by clarifying that the Hīnayāna abandons these seven consciousnesses and four afflictions,
it is therefore called "distinguishing the Hīnayāna by means of the Mahāyāna."

The reason why the seven consciousnesses and four afflictions are not explained for those of the Hīnayāna is that these seven consciousnesses are universal consciousnesses that are difficult to understand; therefore,
they are not taught in the Hīnayāna teachings.
Because it does not teach the existence of the seven consciousnesses,
those of the Hīnayāna school maintain that all afflictions reside within the six consciousnesses; likewise,
the practitioners of the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya* maintain that associated ignorance resides among the mental factors (*caitta*) associated with the six consciousnesses.
The followers of the *Tattvasiddhi* maintain that the nature of grasping ignorance resides in the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍvijñāna*).
The Mahāyāna followers state that this associated nature of grasping also exists in the seventh consciousness (*saptavijñāna*).
Because this principle exists, it is necessary to employ it to distinguish their [respective] small [vehicles].
First, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* distinguishes five stages:
first, the stage of the external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*);
second, the stage of the internal ordinary person (*adhyātmikapṛthagjana*).
From the four applications of mindfulness upward,
three stages are called the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga).
From the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti) upward...
The fourth is the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*),
which refers to the states from the sixteenth moment of mind onwards.
The fifth is called the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
This refers to those from the stage of Arhat upward;
during the initial stage of an ordinary person outside the [Holy] Path,
one cultivates the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and meditation regarding the phenomena of the three realms.
At that time, the active manifestations (*paryavasthāna*) of the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) within the stages of the six consciousnesses are subdued and severed;
however, the active manifestations of the four delusions of the *ādānavijñāna* still persist.
This refers to the stage from the second application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) upward.
Within the stage of the inner ordinary person,
one trains in the contemplation of non-self, which is able to suppress the active manifestations of *dharma-ātman* and *pudgala-ātman* views.
Question:
The view of self arises based on the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
Since practitioners of the two vehicles and those at the stage of ordinary beings have not yet perceived the fundamental consciousness,
how could they possibly suppress or eliminate the view of self in the seven consciousnesses?
The commentary states:
Ordinary beings are deluded regarding the general characteristics of the seven consciousnesses and the five aggregates, taking them to be the self.

The Sage, speaking according to principle, explains that the essential nature of the five aggregates is the fundamental consciousness; this is the principle of designating the *ālayavijñāna* as the basis.
When the mind of self-view arises, it does not at that time take the ālayavijñāna as its intentional object;
rather, it takes the "self-as-object" (ātma-viṣaya) as its intentional object.
Nevertheless, this may still be termed "arising by taking the fundamental consciousness as its condition."
Within the stage of the ordinary person (pṛthagjana), one contemplates those dharmas of the five aggregates as their common characteristic and forms the understanding that they are non-self;
yet, one is still unable to specifically discern the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna).
Although it is not specifically discerned, the substance of the five aggregates that serve as the object of perception is, in fact, the fundamental consciousness.
Because one contemplates the five aggregates as being without self, this is also called contemplating the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) as being without self;
thus, one is able to suppress the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*).
Third is the stage of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
From the stage of patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) upward,
one is able to permanently sever the functional seeds of the four afflictions (*kleśa*) abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*),
as well as the functional seeds of the ten afflictions abandoned by the path of seeing within the fundamental consciousness.
Regarding the fourth stage, the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*):
from the sixteenth moment of mind upward until the stage of *anāgāmin*,
there are two meanings concerning the seeds of the four afflictions that are severed by the Vajra-like Samādhi during the Path of Cultivation.
First, regarding the analysis of the four afflictions at a distinct time:
one merely severs the seeds of the three afflictions— self-love (*ātmasneha*), self-conceit (*asmimāna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*)—
because the preceding [afflictions] have not yet been fully severed.
I have already severed the seeds of the view of self; they are not severed again now.
Second, regarding the simultaneous fourfold afflictions of discrimination:
one severs the seeds of those four afflictions of the path of cultivation.
It also severs the seeds of the four underlying tendencies—greed, hatred, delusion, and pride—among the ten underlying tendencies.
The former meaning is as explained in the "Chapter on Various Names.
There are three types of persons within the True Dharma.
The first is called right reflection,
which pertains to the four foundations of mindfulness;
the second is called right cultivation.
Those above the stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata) are called the three types of those in training (śaikṣa).
Those above the stage of "Patience regarding Suffering" (duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti) [are those beyond training].
The first two subdue the view of self,
while the latter one eradicates the view of self;
yet, although this contradicts the body, the craving for a self constantly persists within the fundamental consciousness.
Furthermore, from the perspective that the seeds of the four afflictions cultivated on the path share the same essence, they are all termed "self-love" (ātmasneha),
which is similar to the latter definition.
The *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*, in the chapter on Cultivation and Abiding, states:
In the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), non-perverted dharmas and perverted dharmas are intermingled according to their respective conditions.
On the level of external ordinary beings, the latent state of the self-view of the six consciousnesses is called "conforming to the non-perverted";
its association with the self-view within the seventh consciousness is called "intermingling with the perverted."

In the stage of the inner ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), the four afflictions (*kleśa*) that lie dormant within the seven consciousnesses are called "conforming to non-inversion" (*anābhogānupravṛtti*);
their association with the seeds of these four afflictions is termed "intermingling.
For the two types of noble learners (*śaikṣa-ārya*), they are pursued by inversions.

The persistence of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the four delusions abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), along with the persistence of the seeds of the four proclivities (*anuśaya*), is called "being pursued by inversions.

When the seeds of the four delusions abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*) and the seeds of six among the ten proclivities have been eliminated, it is called "the absence of inverted views."
At the stage of the external ordinary level, the four afflictions are universally defiled;
these are the afflictions of both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation arising in ordinary persons.
Upon entering the path of seeing, one severs only the seeds of the afflictions of the truth of seeing.
The habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the four proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the path of cultivation have not yet been severed.
Therefore, while the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) severs only the seeds of the four afflictions consisting of defiled afflictions of the truths (*satyadarśana-kleśa*),
it does not sever the habitual tendencies of the four afflictions consisting of defiled afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga-kleśa*).
The three types of those beyond training (aśaikṣa) are called "non-erroneous" (aviparyāsa).
They are followed by non-erroneous dharmas;
that which is free from the four delusions regarding the truths and so forth is termed "non-erroneous."
In the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the seeds of the four proclivities (*anuśaya*) are called "non-perverted accompaniments.
In the stage beyond that of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), there remain only residual habitual tendencies of the seeds.

In the fifth stage, that of no-more-learning, from the Arhat upward, there exist only the residual habitual tendencies of the seeds of the four afflictions (*kleśa*) and the residual habitual tendencies of the seeds of the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*).
Furthermore, there are no longer the active manifestations of the four afflictions (*kleśa*) or the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*);

rather, there remain only the seeds and residual habits of the four afflictions, as well as the seeds and residual habits among the ten proclivities, within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
This causes arhats and others to give rise to attachments such as "my robe" and "my bowl" even within an indeterminate state of mind;
these residual seeds of habituation are not severed by the two vehicles,
whereas they are eliminated in the Mahāyāna.
If the noble ones of the two vehicles do not sever the seeds of the four afflictions in their active state (*samudācāra*),
then among the ten fetters (*daśa-ānuśaya*), the seed of the view of self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) in its active state should likewise not be severed. Why is this?
Because they arise with the same object-condition as the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
Therefore, the "Chapter on the Object-Condition" (*Ālambanavibhāga*) states:
"The *ālayavijñāna*, the *ādānavijñāna*, and the sixth consciousness..."
I perceive the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) as having the objects of the six consciousnesses as its conditions.
Since it takes the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) as its common object-condition,
why do you selectively sever the view of self in the six consciousnesses while not severing the self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*) in the seventh consciousness?
It is judged that there is no such principle.
Furthermore, the four afflictions of the seventh consciousness constitute the substance of the obstacle of the self-view (pudgala-dṛṣṭi).
If a sage did not sever these four afflictions, [he would remain bound].
The noble beings of the two vehicles should not sever the substance of the obstacle of the person-self;
for the *anāgāmin* and *arhat*, there is no *dāna* (giving) in the higher mind whether entering or emerging [from meditative absorption],
but it can only exist within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
Furthermore, within the miscellaneous mental states (*miśra-citta*), the ignorance that clings to those *dhāna* is identified as the associated ignorance (*saṃprayukta-avidyā*).
Associated ignorance is subject to abandonment through both the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Thus, it is determined that the seeds and residual habits of these four afflictions are subject to abandonment through both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.
The analysis of the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* is concluded.
Next, the analysis of the stages of the *Tattvasiddhi* consists of five distinct parts.
The first is the stage of the external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*).
Prior to the stage of dry wisdom (śuṣka-vipaśyanā),
these two are called the "inner ordinary beings" (adhyātma-prthagjana);
from the stages of hearing and reflection (śruta-cintā) upward, they are [the noble ones].
The first three are the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
From the signless (*animitta*) stage upward,
the next four are the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
From the stage of the Sakṛdāgāmin upward,
the fifth is called the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣamārga).
This refers to those from the Arhat upward.
The first stage of the external ordinary person has not yet entered the Ground of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*).
They merely suppress the active manifestations of the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) within the six consciousnesses.
Within the Ground of Dry Wisdom, they suppress the active manifestations of the four delusions (*kleśa*) within the *manas* consciousness.

In the second stage of the inner ordinary person (*prthagjana*), which consists of the levels of hearing and reflection (*śruta-maya* and *cintā-maya*), one abandons the view of a self that is merely conventional;
once the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī prajñā*) is attained and above, one abandons the view of a self that is substantially real.
Therefore, that treatise states:
Delusions of conventional designation are extinguished through the causes and conditions of extensive learning,
or through the causes and conditions of contemplation.
Delusions of ultimate reality are extinguished within the stages of Heat and Summits.
This untainted mind of liberation correctly severs the seeds of ignorance within the seven consciousnesses and also severs the ten fetters and the ignorance abandoned through seeing.
Within the third stage, the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), the two types of delusion— provisional and substantial— are severed to their ultimate end.
Therefore, that treatise states:
"From the stage of *ūṣmagata* onwards, one gradually abandons the afflictions until they are exhausted through the vision of cessation (*nirodha*).
This means that within the state of the non-characteristic (*animitta*), the general realization of the emptiness of intrinsic nature is termed the "vision of cessation."
In the fourth stage, that of the Path of Cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), one eliminates the seeds and residual habits of those four delusions;
one also eliminates the four proclivities (anuśaya) of the path of cultivation.
These are likewise termed "residual habits" in contrast to the delusions of the path of seeing (darśana-heya).
According to the *Tattvasiddhi* school, within the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there is no further grasping at intrinsic nature.
Judging by the intent of this passage,
the four afflictions (*kleśa*) should not arise as active mental states (*paryavasthāna*).
It can only give rise to those four latent dispositions (anuśaya) in their subtle form;

it can also arise within a mind associated with outflows (sāsrava-citta). In the fifth stage, that of the Arhat (aśaikṣa-bhūmi), there exist only the seeds of the four afflictions within the foundational consciousness (ālayavijñāna) as subtle residual habits.
What differs from the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* is that within the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the residual habits are severed;
in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣabhūmi*), there remain only seeds and subtle residual habits.
There is this distinction.
Thus, the *Nirākāra-śāstra* states:
"Arhats possess only residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*)."

The explanation of the Great Vehicle and the completion of the Small Vehicle is finished. Second, regarding the explanation of the stages of cultivation and abandonment within the Mahāyāna, there are five positions.
The first is the stage of the external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*), called the ground of constant submersion.
The second inner ordinary person is named the stage of the ten faiths;
the third is the stage of the ten understandings and the ten practices;
the fourth is the ten transferences and the ten stages.
The fifth is the Buddha-ground.
First, regarding external ordinary persons (*bāla-pṛthagjana*), they are constantly submerged in the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) that manifest as afflictions;
within their wholesome or neutral states of mind, these ten proclivities do not manifest.
Since there are only four afflictions that manifest in the active mind,
the *Zhòngmíng zhāng* states:
"They pervade the minds of ordinary beings, whether virtuous, non-virtuous, or indeterminate."
Within the second stage of the inner ordinary person, the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), there are two kinds of bodhisattvas.
The first is called the bodhisattva of sudden enlightenment (*tunwu pusa*);
he merely suppresses the active manifestations (*ūrdhvabhūmika*) of the four delusions and the active manifestations of the ten latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Because the seeds of the four delusions, the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*), and the latent tendencies have not yet been severed.
As stated in the "Chapter on the Cultivation of the Fifth Superior Phase":
"The stage of the Ten Faiths is called the indeterminate *asaṃkhyeya*."
There are white dharmas that are mixed with black;
they are no different from those of ordinary worldlings.
World-transcending, outflow-tainted wholesome states are called white dharmas.
Because of the residual habits of the seeds of the four delusions and the seeds of the ten fetters,
the *Awakening of Faith* states:
"The defilement associated with attachment."
Because it is removed through the liberation of the two vehicles and the stage of faith-correspondence (*adhimukti-saṃprayukta-bhūmi*),
the seeds of those four afflictions (*kleśa*) and the seeds of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) within the six consciousnesses are termed the "defilement associated with attachment" (*saṃyoga-kleśa*).
Verifying this single passage,
one certainly knows that the four afflictions are exhausted only upon becoming an Arhat;
thus, those such as Arhats are liberated through the vehicle of the two vehicles.
Because they have attained both liberation through mind and liberation through wisdom,
there are two types of bodhisattvas within the third stage, the Stage of Ten Understandings (*daśa-vijñapti-bhūmi*).

If it is a bodhisattva of sudden enlightenment who reaches this Stage of Ten Understandings, they sever the seeds of the active outflows (*paryavasthāna*) of the four afflictions as well as the seeds of the ten active outflows.
Therefore, the "Chapter on Cultivation" states:
"The ten stages of understanding and the ten stages of practice are called the fixed asaṃkhyeya;
they consist of neither-black-nor-white dharmas mixed with white dharmas."
The untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) consisting of the contemplation of the non-self of persons is called the "neither-black-nor-white dharma.
Worldly tainted wholesome states (*laukika-sāsrava-kuśala*) are called "white dharmas.
That which arises between these two is termed "mixed."
Because one has attained the untainted liberation of the non-self of persons,
one is able to counteract the four delusions, the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*), and the seeds of the primary proclivities.
This practice arises based on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Second, the Bodhisattvas of gradual enlightenment, upon reaching the stages of the Ten Understandings and the Ten Practices, are able to counteract the residual habits of the seeds of the four delusions of discrimination as well as the residual habits of the seeds of the ten afflictions.
Therefore, the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* states:
"As for the 'affliction associated with non-interruption,' one abandons it through the skillful means of the stage of faith-correspondence, up until the stage of the pure mind."

The residual habits of the seeds of the four afflictions and the residual habits of the seeds of the ten fetters within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) are termed "affliction associated with non-interruption" (*asaṃprayukta-kleśa*).

In the fourth stage, the tenth stage, and throughout the ten stages (*bhūmi*), one severs the residual habits of the seeds of the four afflictions and the residual habits of the seeds of the ten fetters, as well as severing the ignorance-abiding ground (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*) of attachment to dharmas.
Therefore, the *Nirābhāsa-śāstra* states:

"The active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) and their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), as well as the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the afflictions abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*), are severed only by the wisdom that accords with suchness (*tathatā-jñāna*).
The residual habits of the seeds of the four delusions and the residual habits of the seeds of the ten fetters (*daśa-saṃyojana*) are termed 'habitual tendencies'."
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
"For Bodhisattvas of the ten stages, the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) that they have severed are all merely residual habits.
The fifth chapter on "Superior Characteristics" says:
The nature of ignorance of ordinary beings is the ignorance of conceptualizing a self in phenomena (*dharma-ātman-vikalpa-avidyā*).
It is abandoned upon reaching the tenth stage of the *bhūmis* and entering the first stage.
This practice arises based on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Because the Bodhisattva has severed the grasping at a person and a self (*pudgala-ātma-grāha*), their practice is not the same as that of the Two Vehicles.
Although the followers of the Two Vehicles take the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as their object and form the understanding of non-self, [they do not sever the grasping at a person].
Not knowing that the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) are their fundamental consciousness (mūla-vijñāna),
the bodhisattva contemplates the five aggregates and forms the understanding of non-self (anātman).
[Only when] able to know that the five aggregates are their fundamental consciousness [does he truly understand].
Furthermore, while those of the two vehicles practice the contemplation of *dharmalakṣaṇa* (characteristics of phenomena), the Bodhisattva practices that contemplation of signlessness (*animitta*).

Knowing that both the self and objects are signless, and that there is only the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), he performs the contemplation of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) within the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmaśūnyatā*) from the tenth stage (*daśamī-bhūmi*) upward.

It is called the Wisdom of Suchness (tathatājñāna), which can extinguish habitual tendencies (vāsanā) and eliminate grasping; at the fifth Buddha-ground, the residual impressions of the seeds of the four delusions, the residual impressions of the seeds of the ten afflictions (anuśaya), and all forms of attachment to phenomena and self (dharmātman-grāha) are entirely exhausted.
Therefore, the fifth chapter, "The World-transcending Purity," states:
"When the four virtues are perfected, the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is entirely exhausted;
all impure aspects of the fundamental consciousness—afflictions, karma, and suffering—are completely extinguished."
Chapter Four: The Meaning of Impregnation (*vāsanā*). This is extracted from the "Chapter on the Manifestation of the Primary Superior Characteristics" (*Prathamavaiśeṣikalakṣaṇanirdeśaparivarta*).
As for what is called "impregnation," it is the very basis of both the real and the false.
As the primary gateway to both defilement and purity,
it establishes the delusory to reveal the true;
there is nothing that is not encompassed by this.
Defilement arises and purity emerges;
both the provisional and the real depend upon the same basis.
Therefore, both the sutras and the śāstras describe this essential point together.
The meaning of perfuming (*vāsanā*) is analyzed through eight sections:
first, the explanation of the etymological meaning;
second, the clarification of its essential nature and boundaries.
Third, the distinction in the meaning of perfuming;
fourth, the analysis according to stages;
fifth, the analysis of the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
Sixth, the distinction between the outflowing and the outflow-free;
seventh, the distinction between the ordinary person and the noble one;
eighth, the distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles.
Regarding the explanation of the etymological meanings:
the coarse [elements] nourishing the subtle are termed "perfuming" (vāsanā),
while the subtle [elements] maintaining the coarse portions are designated as "habituation" (abhyāsa).
There are four types of perfuming (vāsanā), which differ from one another:
first, that which serves as a support for perfuming;
second, that which constitutes the perfuming itself.
Third is perfuming by transformation;
fourth is perfuming by manifestation.
Regarding what is called "sustaining perfuming":
The mutual assistance provided by phenomena such as the real and the false is termed "mutual perfuming" (*zixun*).
Therefore, in the *Awakening of Faith*,
it is referred to as the "perfuming of True Suchness" (*zhēnrú xūnxùn zhēnrú*) and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "perfumed into existence":

when the sixth and seventh consciousnesses give rise to defiled or pure states, they perfume the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna), thereby forming defiled or pure seeds; this is what is meant by "perfumed into existence.
Therefore, the *Vāsanā-prakaraṇa* (Chapter on Perfuming) states:
